Breaking.title: Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war
Breaking.text:
There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground.

For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.

With a diameter of just over a metre there is enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line – and make it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.

Going underground is now the "only option", says Zanuda, who has helped plan Ukraine's tunnel operation and calls it a new world of fighting. But, he acknowledges, it is hard.

"On the surface you always have some room to manoeuvre, but here you can only engage the enemy head-on."

The journey to get to this subterranean battleground in the Kharkiv region only reinforced the dangers on the ground: a high-speed move by vehicle across open fields, followed by a long march across muddy ground – accompanied by Ukrainian troops with their weapons loaded, ready to shoot down Russian drones.

Arriving at the tunnel entrance, the first thing to hit you is the lingering smell of gas and fetid air.

Both sides use openings in the pipeline to get to the surface, where most of the fighting takes place. They have made breaches in the ground, and used welding tools to break through the thick steel.

The Russians were the first to exploit the pipe to infiltrate the nearby city of Kupyansk in September 2025. They have used underground pipelines before, during the capture of the city of Avdiivka in 2024, and last year in their bid to recapture areas of Russia's Kursk region.

But Ukrainian forces have slowly turned the tables.

A specially designed electric cart transports troops and supplies through the pipeline.

They call it the Kupyansk metro. It occasionally breaks down. We travelled on it for 40 minutes, heads bowed and legs crossed. There is a regular bump as you cross the welded sections of the pipe. It is like an austere fairground ride, without the fun.

Our destination was a break in the pipeline where Ukrainian troops have built dug-outs to store ammunition and equipment, with just enough room to stand. It is where the man they call Musician conducts the movement of troops and supplies. He has been living like a mole, his face engrained with dirt and earth.

Musician tells me he has spent the past three months there, with a few brief visits above ground to clean up or go to the toilet. From time to time we can hear the thuds of artillery rounds above. Musician tells me we are close to the line of contact: "But it's safe underground."

The cart continues its journey into the bowels of the earth. It returns about half an hour later with more troops covered in dirt. They have been fighting in positions on the surface.

There is a look of relief on their dust-caked faces.

"It's more comfortable in the pipe because drones don't fly here, and neither do artillery shells or glide bombs," says Vovochka, who has been fighting on the ground for the past three weeks.

But there has been fighting in the pipeline, too. Operation Veles, named after a mythical Slavic god of the underworld, began in April. Since then Ukraine has advanced 15km (9.3 miles) along the pipeline.

It has been painstaking, backbreaking work – with the ever-present fear of coming into contact with the enemy.

Back above ground we meet a few of the soldiers, from the 13th Khartiia Brigade of Ukraine's National Guard, who have taken part in the mission. Their first task was to clear the detritus, water and Russian barricades inside the pipeline.

The Ukrainian troops say some of the barriers were boobytrapped or piled with Russian bodies. "When we moved them or climbed over them, we had no idea what was underneath," says Chyzh.

The other danger, he said, was the ricochets from gunfire when they tried to advance. "You never know where a bullet is going to go or how it will bounce."

His comrade Kort says "we were all firing, we were pushing them back". Over the course of the operation Ukraine says it killed more than 100 Russian soldiers and took 30 prisoners. "Yes, there were bodies," says Kort. "I even had to sleep right next to them."

While some of the fighting taking place underground, there are still battles on the surface and in the air. It has been a combined operation.

But Zanuda, who is chief of the planning section of the 13th Khartiia Brigade, believes it is the best way to fight in the future. "Ground operations are now nearly impossible," he said, adding that "everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground".

There'll be more missions like this, he believes. "Pipelines run everywhere," he said. "You have to remember, back in the Soviet times, oil, gas and ammonia were being transported to Europe, with the entire transit route running through Ukraine."

In reality it has been brutal, gruelling and dangerous work in the harshest of conditions.

It has taken Ukraine seven months to clear 15km of the pipeline.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has hailed it as a success.

It has helped retake lost territory and been a boost for morale, but on its own it has not changed the course of the war.

Additional reporting by Moose Campbell, Volodymyr Lozhko and Rebecca Hartmann

Breaking.title: Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin
Breaking.text:
The meeting hasn't even happened yet.

But Thursday's mini summit of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping already looks like a win for the Kremlin.

Whatever the outcome.

Think back to 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine President Putin was an international pariah. Western leaders were determined to isolate him and his country over the war in Ukraine.

Fast forward to 2026: Vladimir Putin has secured an historic meeting in Shenzhen. For the first time in history, the leaders of China, Russia and the United States will sit down – just the three of them – for talks.

That puts Putin exactly where he wants to be: at the top table of global politics, rubbing shoulders with the leaders of the two great powers.

It allows him to boast that Western pressure on Russia has failed.

"We see such examples in the failed attempts to isolate our country, Russia, which has faced unprecedented sanctions pressure," Putin told a business forum of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation organisation.

That was followed by a meeting with Xi Jinping.

But the Kremlin says the "showstopper" event in Shenzhen will be Putin's trilateral with Xi and Trump.

It allows him to play global statesman, even as the Russian military continues to pound Ukrainian towns and cities, and the Kremlin continues to reject the idea of an unconditional, comprehensive ceasefire.

One short meeting is unlikely to reshape the world. But it's the optics that are key. The picture. The photo-op. Three leaders, three big powers, discussing big issues.

In a way, Vladimir Putin will use this meeting to send a holiday postcard to the rest of the world. Instead of "Wish you were here", he'll sign it: "Look: I'm here."

But what of those who are not at the table?

Among European leaders, and especially in Ukraine, there is concern that the three-way meeting might produce more than just a pretty picture, though not in a good way for Kyiv.

Donald Trump has already said that in Shenzhen he wants to discuss his "favourite subject" - the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin would likely welcome an opportunity to argue its case to Trump and Xi without Ukrainian officials or European leaders in the room.

Last month Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed concern that the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting might resemble the Yalta Conference of 1945. That is when the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States – Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt - met to re-organise post-World War Two Europe.

"We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence," said Zelensky.

It is unclear whether China would want the Ukraine war on the agenda in Shenzhen. In its official statements on the upcoming trilateral meeting, Beijing has talked more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".

In Shenzhen, Russia will make the most of the optics. But a diplomatic victory is not the same as a military one.

Nearly five years after President Putin launched his so-called "special military operation", Russia is still struggling to win its war on Ukraine.

Over this time, it has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.

And the Ukrainian strike on the road bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula – carried out on the eve of the summit - was a blow to Moscow's prestige. The attack severely damaged part of the multi-billion-dollar bridge built by Russia after it annexed Crimea from Ukraine.

The damage is not only a logistical headache for the Russian authorities.

It is a reminder that the Kremlin's "special operation" has not gone at all to plan.

The Shenzhen summit may give Vladimir Putin a big stage, and a bright spotlight.

It does not necessarily bring him closer to winning the war.

Breaking.title: Birmingham City Council wins legal fight against flags on lamp-posts
Breaking.text:
Birmingham City Council has won a High Court injunction preventing unauthorised flags being attached to lamp-posts and other highway infrastructure across the city.

The authority sought the order after thousands of St George's flags and union jacks were put up by supporters of anti-migrant group Raise the Colours from summer 2025 onwards.

Council lawyers argued the displays created safety risks and fuelled tensions, while campaigners said the move would restrict freedom of expression.

Judge Emma Kelly said there was a "compelling need" to grant the interim injunction.

In her ruling, the judge said it would last until trial or further order of the court.

The order applies to Raise the Colours' leader Ryan Bridge; Ben Cullen, who is also associated with the group; and persons unknown from attaching flags to street furniture and highway infrastructure.

It also grants a power of arrest against Bridge and persons unknown, meaning police could arrest someone without a warrant if they are suspected of breaching the injunction.

The council said anyone who breaches the order could be jailed for up to two years, fined or have their assets seized for contempt of court.

The local authority sought the injunction after thousands of St George's flags and union flags were attached to lamp-posts and bridges in Birmingham from summer 2025 onwards.

Lawyers acting for the council argued the displays could pose safety risks, obstruct visibility and contribute to tensions and disorder. The application also referred to reported incidents of alleged intimidation, harassment and obstruction connected to flags being put up in the city.

The court heard that, on one occasion, a man suffered a broken leg when he was struck by a cherry picker being used while flags were being installed.

Breaking.title: Police investigate death of boy, 3, after nursery incident
Breaking.text:
An investigation has been launched into the death of a three-year-old boy following an incident at a nursery in Greater Manchester, police said.

The boy became critically ill at Cosy Toes Nursery in Middleton shortly before 16:00 GMT on Monday 2 November.

He was rushed to hospital, where he died three days later.

Greater Manchester Police said his family were being supported by specialist officers.

Det Ch Insp Claire Brennan said: "This is an incredibly tragic development in a deeply upsetting incident and our thoughts remain with the boy's family."

Police said an investigation had been launched in line with standard procedure following a child's death in a care setting.

No arrests have been made at this time.

A spokeswoman for Cosy Toes said they were "all heartbroken" by the "wonderful and beautiful" boy's death.

"Our thoughts and prayers are all with his family at this terrible time," she said.

"We will of course give our fullest possible assistance in every way possible to the enquiries that must rightly follow this tragic event."

Anyone with information about the boy's death is being urged to contact police.

Brennan said: "We are in the very early stages of our involvement and are carefully considering events and the evidence available to us.

"For now, we ask that the family's privacy is respected as they begin to navigate the unimaginable loss of their little boy."

Ofsted said it had taken the decision to suspend the nursery's registration in the wake of the incident, meaning the nursery will be closed for six weeks as investigations are carried out.

A spokesperson said: "Our thoughts are with the family of the young boy and everyone affected by this deeply distressing and tragic incident.

"We have worked closely with the police, and we have suspended the nursery's registration. We will continue to support the police and other agencies in their enquiries. We are unable to comment further while the police investigation is ongoing."

Breaking.title: William and Kate reflect on 'enduring' UK-India ties with Modi
Breaking.text:
The Prince and Princess of Wales have met with Prime Minister Narendra Modi to reflect on the enduring ties between the UK and India, as they wrapped up their three-day visit to the country.

William and Catherine arrived in New Delhi on Wednesday for the final leg of their first official overseas trip together in four years.

The meeting was a late addition to the couple's schedule and came after Modi confirmed he would be back from a scheduled trip to the Philippines in time to see the royals.

It comes a day after the royal couple were in Mumbai for the annual Earthshot Prize, which was founded by the prince and remains one of his biggest personal projects.

A Kensington Palace spokesperson said the royals and Modi discussed the "strength and importance of the UK–India bilateral relationship, reflecting on the deep and enduring ties between the two countries and the opportunities to strengthen their partnership in the years ahead".

The prince and princess also spoke "warmly" of their time in the country, thanking the prime minister and the people for their welcome, and added how much they enjoyed returning to India, a decade after their last visit.

Modi called it a "pleasure" to meet them, and said he looks forward to "further strengthening" the India-UK partnership for the "shared prosperity of the people of our nations and the wider world".

The couple last met the Indian prime minister on their official visit to India in 2016.

When Prince William announced earlier this year that The Earthshot Prize ceremony was going to be held in India for the first time, he highlighted India's leadership in climate innovation, its biodiversity and its massive youth population as the key reasons for choosing the country.

Breaking.title: Regulator mistakenly sent complaints about doctors to newspaper
Breaking.text:
The doctors' regulator the General Medical Council (GMC) has apologised after it mistakenly sent information about more than 220 doctors to a national newspaper.

The information included summaries of complaints alleging antisemitism or Islamophobia against the doctors.

For some of the medics involved, it was only when the GMC alerted them to the data breach that they discovered a complaint had been made about them.

The GMC says it is "very sorry" for the incident and has reported itself to the Information Commissioner's Office.

The GMC - an independent body that regulates doctors, physician associates and anaesthesia associates to protect patient safety - sent the information about 223 doctors to a journalist at the Times newspaper.

While no names were revealed, GMC identification numbers were included, which would easily allow doctors to be found on the regulator's register.

Some doctors have also raised concerns that their ethnicity was included in the data breach.

All the medics involved have been the subject of a complaint involving either antisemitism or Islamophobia, dating from the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023 to September 2026.

The GMC says it has a legal and statutory responsibility to investigate such claims.

Meanwhile, the Times is understood to have promised not to make any of the leaked details public, but has said it will not delete the leaked information.

A spokesman for the doctor's trade union, the British Medical Association (BMA), condemned the leak.

"The BMA is aware that a number of doctors have received communication from the GMC to say that it erroneously sent personal identifiable data about them to the Times newspaper when responding to a media request," it said.

"The GMC must take action to ensure such a breach never occurs again."

The BMA said it would look at ways to support members affected and urged them to make contact via their website.

A doctors' campaign group, The Doctors' Association UK (DAUK), called for an independent investigation into the leak.

"If a doctor sent identifiable patient information to a newspaper, they could expect to be referred to the GMC," said Dr Matt Kneale, DAUK co-chairman.

"The GMC should hold itself to the same standard of confidentiality it expects from doctors. It owes every affected doctor a clear account of what it sent, how that happened and what it is doing to get the information deleted."

Breaking.title: Russell Brand: Deputy Labour leader criticises media for 'amplifying' prison message
Breaking.text:
Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell has criticised media organisations for broadcasting a message from the wife of jailed rapist Russell Brand on his behalf.

Laura Brand read out the message on the disgraced comedian's YouTube channel on Sunday, in which he said he was not guilty of the offences for which he is serving a 10-and-a-half year prison sentence.

The message has prompted an official investigation into whether Brand broke prison rules.

The clip of Laura Brand has been played on outlets including BBC Radio 4's Today programme, ITV's This Morning, Sky News, LBC and the News Agents podcast. On Wednesday, Education Secretary Powell said the media should not have "amplified" his words.

"I was appalled at that [message] and actually I think mainstream media shouldn't have transmitted that either," she told LBC on Wednesday.

"It's a platform I don't think should have been amplified, to be honest."

Powell went on to describe Russell Brand as "someone who's not showing a jot of remorse, a jot of any sensitivity at all to their victims".

She continued: "This is somebody who's been convicted and found guilty of very, very serious offences and rape."

In a statement, the BBC said the Today programme had played the Laura Brand clip "in error, due to miscommunication within the team", and had since removed it from catch-up service BBC Sounds.

BBC News has asked the other outlets named above for a comment.

ITN News chief executive Ian Rumsey told BBC Radio 4's The Media Show that the company's newsrooms, including ITV News and Channel 4 News, took the decision not to play the video.

He said: "You didn't need to show it. You could discuss, you could describe what it was, and I'm very pleased and proud that every area of ITN chose not to show it at all, and I think that's exactly the right decision."

YouTube said it is aware of the video and investigating, and that Brand's channel on the platform hasn't been able to make money since being suspended from its advert revenue scheme for "violating" its "creator responsibility policy" after allegations against him emerged in 2023. But the channel is still available to view.

Brand's social media accounts on Meta platforms - which owns Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - were disabled last week.

Earlier this week, Downing Street officials described Brand's message to his followers as "clearly appalling", adding that it was being urgently investigated.

No 10 said it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.

Asked about the message, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.

"Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments."

Breaking.title: Trump shakes hands with Putin and Xi ahead of historic talks in China
Breaking.text:
Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met for the first time in more than a year on Wednesday, as they prepared for landmark talks in China with Xi Jinping.

The US president was greeted off his plane by the Chinese leader as he arrived in Shenzhen for a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders, which will culminate in a closely-watched meeting between the pair and the Russian president.

After a carefully choreographed handshake and hug between Trump and Xi on the tarmac, the US president later greeted and exchanged pleasantries with Putin ahead of a reception.

Trump and Putin are expected to hold one-on-one talks on the sidelines of the summit on Thursday, in which the war in Ukraine could be discussed.

However the main focus during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (Apec) will be on the US-China-Russia talks on Thursday - the first time the trio of leaders have met together in person.

A full agenda has not been made public but there have been various hints about what could be discussed, including the wars in Ukraine and Iran, nuclear proliferation, trade tensions and developments in artificial intelligence.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin and Trump have not yet held a substantive meeting, and merely greeted each other on Wednesday.

Peskov also said that "no more than an hour" had been allocated for Thursday's trilateral talks between Putin, Trump and Xi.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has raised fears of a plan to end the war being discussed in the absence of representatives from Kyiv or Europe.

It is unclear whether China would want this issue to be on the agenda in Shenzhen, with Beijing talking more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".

China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.

Wednesday's handshake was the first in-person meeting between Trump and Putin since August 2025, when the Russian leader travelled to Alaska for talks on the Ukraine war which failed to deliver a breakthrough.

Xi's personal reception for Trump at the airport mimicked a similar move by the US president when the Chinese leader visited Washington in September, a gesture Xi described as "special".

In Shenzhen, a red carpet was rolled out in front of Air Force One for Trump, with a cheering crowd, honour guard, military flyover and flowers presentation all in place to welcome him.

Chinese state-run news agency Xinhua quoted Xi as saying he wanted to pursue a "constructive strategic and stable relationship based on respect, fairness, and equality".

Xi's greeting will be seen as a diplomatic gesture designed to begin the week's talks with his American counterpart on a cordial note.

Breaking.title: Kuwait says it repelled first Iranian attack in two months after US strikes island
Breaking.text:
Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.

The drone attack on Kuwait was the first in more than two months. The Iranian army said it had targeted the Ali Al Salem Airbase, which hosts US forces, but Kuwaiti authorities did not report any damage.

It came after US warplanes struck an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to US military officials.

Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates' state oil firm said a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf waterway on Tuesday.

The recent exchanges of fire, as well as deadlock in negotiations on a peace deal, have raised fears of a major escalation in the nine-month-old war.

The conflict began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.

Since then, Iran has retaliated for US and Israeli strikes by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.

It has also attacked dozens of commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass.

On Tuesday night, Kuwait's military said its air defences engaged "drone threats" but did not report any casualties or damage.

The Kuwaiti foreign ministry condemned the attack, saying it "flagrantly violated Kuwait's sovereignty, directly threatened its security and stability, and constituted a grave breach of international law".

"The explosions seemed to be coming from far away, but hearing them again after a period of calm was both surprising and worrying," Hani Mohammed, an Egyptian resident of Kuwait, told AFP news agency.

Bahrain's military also said on Wednesday that its air defence systems had "intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks".

The island kingdom, which hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet, has reported four attacks over the past six days, following a two-month lull.

Qatar, which has mediated in the stalled indirect talks between Iran and the US, said the Iranian attacks on its neighbours were a "dangerous escalation that threatens to complicate efforts aimed at containing tensions".

The Iranian army said its drones had targeted US Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait.

Later, the army's commander-in-chief, Maj Gen Amir Hatami, warned the US and its allies that it would respond more forcefully to any new attacks on Iran.

"If the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations," he said.

On Tuesday night, US fighter jets targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm Island "with precision munitions" in response to Iranian "aggression targeting US personnel and assets", US military officials said.

Iranian media reported explosions on the island but cited a local official as saying they had caused no damage to infrastructure.

In a separate development, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) said a search-and-rescue operation was under way for a missing sailor following an attack on one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. The rest of the crew were safely evacuated and 11 were receiving medical care, it added.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre reported that a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles (24km) north of Khasab, in Oman's Musandam peninsula. It said the attack caused a fire on board that was extinguished.

Iran said two oil tankers and a ship carrying liquefied natural gas (LNG) had caught fire after hitting naval mines while sailing along an "authorised route".

At least 25 seafarers have been killed across the Middle East since the start of the war, when the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the conflict and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.

In recent months, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling through the Strait of Hormuz, allowing crude oil exports from Gulf states to reach around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts.

Breaking.title: Parents jailed for torture and death of four-year-old girl in France nearly 40 years ago
Breaking.text:
The mother of a four-year-old girl killed in central France and found along a motorway almost 40 years ago has been sentenced to 20 years in prison.

Halima El Bakhti, 72, was found guilty on Tuesday of "torture and acts of barbarity resulting in death without the intent to kill", French media reports.

The girl's father, 74-year-old Ahmed Touloub, was handed a 15-year sentence as an accomplice.

Four-year-old Inass Touloub was found along the A10 road in Suèvres in the Loir-et-Cher department on 11 August 1987. Her body bore multiple marks of abuse, including human bite marks, broken bones and burns with an iron.

She was buried in an unmarked grave near the location where her body was found. Unidentified for three decades, she was known only as the "Little Martyr of the A10".

Then, in 2018, she was identified after the DNA of her brother – tested in an unrelated case – matched with hers, leading to the arrest of their parents.

The trial took place in Loir-et-Cher Assize Court from 2 November, with the verdict delivered on Tuesday after several hours of deliberation.

During the trial, prosecutor Anaïs Allio emphasised that "not a single part of Inass's body was spared", and recalled the "sense of vertigo that overcame us all" upon viewing the "unbearable photographs" from the autopsy, France Info reports.

The jury concluded that the child's mother was suffering from impaired judgement at the time of the girl's death, which reduced the maximum potential sentence.

French media outlet France Info described the two defendants as sitting stoically in chairs before the court with their heads bowed as the reasoning behind the verdict was read out.

El Bakhti and Touloub have 10 days to appeal the verdict.

Inass's death sparked one of France's biggest ever investigations, with the girl's photograph posted in public places and an alert sent to more than 30 countries.

Breaking.title: Falcon 6X: Why Ghana is facing backlash over new $60m presidential jet
Breaking.text:
Ghana's government has defended its purchase of a new presidential jet amid criticism over its cost, as many citizens continue to struggle with the high cost of living.

The $60m (£46m) French-made Falcon 6X has sparked a political row, with opposition politicians accusing President John Mahama's administration of misplaced priorities.

But the government says the purchase is justified, arguing that Ghana's improving economy makes the aircraft affordable and is needed to replace an ageing presidential jet.

The controversy comes as Mahama's administration seeks to demonstrate an economic recovery after years of financial difficulties that forced Ghana to seek IMF assistance.

Manufactured by French aerospace company Dassault Aviation, the aircraft was delivered to the Ghana Air Force on Monday at a reported cost of $61m.

Parliament approved its purchase last December as part of a broader programme to modernise Ghana's military aviation fleet, which also includes four helicopters from Airbus.

The jet was welcomed with a water salute on Monday, but its arrival triggered criticism online and among opposition politicians over the cost and timing of the purchase.

While in the opposition, Mahama himself opposed buying a new presidential jet, prompting questions about why his administration has now gone head with the purchase.

Opposition MP Samuel Abu Jinapor questioned the government's priorities, saying the expenditure came at a time when many Ghanaians continue to struggle with the cost of living and youth unemployment remained alarmingly high.

"What was unacceptable in opposition cannot suddenly become acceptable in government merely because the occupants of power have changed," Jinapor added.

He accused the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) of hypocrisy, recalling how its senior figures had strongly opposed proposals for a new presidential aircraft when they were in opposition.

Jinapor also called for greater transparency over the procurement process, how the purchase was financed and the government's justification for the expenditure.

The purchase has also prompted sharp criticism on social media, with some users arguing the money could have been spent on more pressing public needs.

"This money can employ over 100,000 nurses and 200,000 teachers," an X user posted.

But the government has rejected the criticism, saying Ghana's economic circumstances have changed considerably since the NDC opposed a similar purchase.

Peter Lanchene Toobu, chairman of parliament's defence committee, said the party had never opposed acquiring a presidential jet in principle.

Its objection, he said, had been on the timing when Ghana was experiencing severe economic difficulties.

"We agreed in principle that we needed to purchase a new presidential jet," he said.

He argued, however, that Ghana could not justify the expenditure at a time when it was seeking a $3bn bailout from the IMF.

"The strength and macroeconomic stability of this country have enhanced our status in the sense that imports have become cheaper, and this is the right time," he added.

Toobu said the government had purchased the aircraft without borrowing, citing a stronger Ghanaian currency and improved economic conditions.

Government spokesperson Kwakye Ofosu also dismissed suggestions that the purchase was a misplaced priority.

He pointed to falling prices of construction materials and lower borrowing costs as evidence of the country's improved economic situation.

"When I was campaigning in 2024, and I was donating cement, it cost 115 cedis (£7.5) a bag. Today, for 80 cedis, you will get a bag of cement," he told JoyNews.

The controversy has also extended to the aircraft's interior, following claims that it has a dedicated bedroom and bathroom.

But Ofosu dismissed claims that the jet had such luxury facilities, saying the president has no intention of "bathing in the air".

"There certainly is no bathroom. President Mahama has no intention of bathing in the air," Ofosu said.

He explained that the jet has reclining seats that can be converted into sleeping arrangements but denied that it has a dedicated bedroom.

The government says the new jet will replace the 16-year-old Falcon 900EX, which has suffered recurring maintenance problems, including corrosion and leakages in its fuel tank.

The older jet was reportedly grounded in France for several months in 2025 while undergoing repairs.

Officials say the Falcon 6X has a longer flying range, reducing the need for refuelling stops on international trips and improving the reliability of presidential travel.

Professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin, an economist at the University of Ghana said that while the president's safety was paramount, the timing of the purchase was difficult to justify amid severe austerity measures, high unemployment and widespread infrastructure challenges.

"The timing makes it a bit difficult to understand," he told the BBC, adding that the government should provide a cost-benefit analysis explaining why buying the jet was preferable to leasing one and how the decision serves Ghana's interests.

Additional reporting by Thomas Naadi in Accra

Breaking.title: Hakeem Jeffries nominated to be US Speaker of the House
Breaking.text:
Democrats in the US House of Representatives officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker, setting him on the path to become the first black lawmaker to lead the chamber.

The House will elect its new Speaker on 3 January, when the next term begins and Democrats will be in the majority.

His election to the powerful position - the Speaker is in line to succeed the president after the vice-president - is widely expected. Should he win, Jeffries will preside over his party's largest House majority in years and benefit from the Senate also being under Democrats' control.

Jeffries told reporters after the vote that the nomination was "a high honour and a distinct privilege".

As of Wednesday, Democrats will hold at least 257 seats in the House next year, which is well beyond the 218 needed for a majority. Seven races from the recent midterm elections are still uncalled.

Jeffries, who represents a district in New York, was re-elected as the party leader in a 251-11 closed-door vote on Wednesday. He has served as minority leader since 2023.

Despite overwhelming support in Wednesday's vote, Jeffries faced a handful of holdouts from new members in the party's left wing, who have said the party's sweeping victory in the midterm elections is a sign voters want change.

"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes in this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of our leadership," seven incoming lawmakers, including fellow New Yorkers Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, said in a statement.

All congressional Democrats are gearing up for clashes with the White House once they officially take control in January.

President Donald Trump, a Republican, has signalled a willingness to work with Democrats on some issues, but has also pledged to use his veto power to reject legislation he does not like.

That could make it hard for Democrats to deliver on their campaign promises to address affordability and pass other reforms.

At a news conference following the vote on Wednesday, Jeffries pledged that House Democrats would "fight to lower the high costs of groceries and gas and housing", and "make healthcare affordable for every single American".

Though the party will have a large enough majority to weather defections on must-pass legislation, Jeffries will still have to navigate internal ideological divisions that have grown particularly sharp over US support of Israel and Americans' rising healthcare costs.

Many incoming Democrats, including members of the Democratic Socialists of America, won their elections by challenging the party establishment.

The Congressional Progressive Caucus, from the party's left wing, congratulated Jeffries on the nomination, adding they would "continue conversations with Leader Jeffries to ensure Democrats deliver a bold agenda for working people".

Along with shepherding legislation, Jeffries as Speaker will also have to manage the complex array of investigations that Democrats plan to launch into Trump, his family, and cabinet members now that they have regained control of the chamber's oversight powers.

Rounding out their party leadership team, House Democrats also elected Katherine Clark of Massachusetts as majority leader, Pete Aguilar of California as majority whip, and Joe Neguse of Colorado as assistant speaker.

Business.title: Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as UK inflation rate rises again
Business.text:
Gas and electricity bills for a typical household are forecast to jump by £443 a year from January as the inflation rate rose to its highest level in a year.

A typical annual bill is predicted to rise by 26% in the new year, according to consultancy Cornwall Insight, ahead of the official announcement next week.

Some households will get a £100 payment to help with the rising cost of living, a policy which was announced in the Budget.

Prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices, official figures show.

Inflation has been driven higher in recent months as the US-Israel war with Iran has driven up the cost of energy and fuel.

In response to prices surging, the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years earlier this month, in a bid to slow inflation to its target of 2%.

Interest rates increased from 3.75% to 4%, and the Bank signalled a further rise could be likely unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.

Higher interest rates lift the cost of borrowing for some mortgages, loans and credit cards, but can also lead to a better return on savings.

Emma Reynolds, chief secretary to the Treasury, said the government was providing help for households with energy costs.

VAT has been cut on electricity bills to zero until next July and the government will also hand £100 to 20 million homes in January.

But with annual household energy bills forecast to reach £2,166, Cornwall Insight's retail markets principal, Craig Lowrey, said that "ultimately this support can only chip away at the edges of a bill that continues to be pushed up by events in the Middle East".

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: "Affordability is my number one priority, and I will continue driving towards cheap, clean power."

Business.title: Heating bills, chocolate and cat food: What the inflation figures mean for you
Business.text:
Nobody will be celebrating the fact that prices in the UK are rising at the fastest pace for a year.

Add to that an expectation of higher household energy bills and sharpening price increases and things look grim for everyone.

But there are some signs of hope that may take the edge off the rising cost of living. Here's how.

That headline is not missing a decimal point. The latest prediction for the increase in domestic energy prices in the new year is, indeed, 26%.

Millions of homes in England, Scotland and Wales are on tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap, which is set every three months. The next change for January will be officially announced next Wednesday, 25 November.

Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight, which has a good track record with its predictions, suggests that a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay £2,166 a year - that's an increase of £443 from current levels.

Not all energy use for the year is between January and March, but a big chunk is owing to the cold, dark days and nights.

How much you pay depends on your use, with heavy users of gas likely to be the hardest hit.

The government has promised a £100 payment for people living in homes in council tax bands A to D in England to help cover winter energy costs. Other nations are planning similar support.

The latest inflation data shows that government assistance can have an impact on the general rate of inflation, external, as recorded by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

Domestic energy prices rose by nearly 4% in October, but this was offset in inflationary terms by a cut in VAT on electricity bills.

While the rate of inflation in general was 3.6% in the year to October, food prices only went up by 0.9%.

So why the difference?

It is partly the result of intense competition between the supermarkets. Like many retailers, they are facing higher costs but are not passing that onto their customers in full.

There may be some scars from the recent cost-of-living spike here. Shoppers suffered a period during the big rise in inflation in 2022-23 when food prices rocketed.

Those higher prices are embedded. While food prices overall aren't coming down now, they aren't rising anywhere near as fast as back then.

The detail here is very interesting. Take chocolate: world cocoa prices are down since 2024, and now chocolate prices are falling - down 2.9%, according to the latest data.

But the ONS has also pointed to cat food as one, albeit small, driver of the faster rate of rising prices.

Should high energy and fuel costs - which are driving the rising rate of inflation - persist, there are questions over whether the cost of producing and transporting food also goes up, and the chances of that higher cost being passed on to consumers are greater.

Economists have been closely studying whether there are any signs of those so-called second-round effects - where an initial price shock spreads to wages, services and broader consumer prices. So far, there are relatively few.

Food is, of course, a necessity.

If prices rise then it takes a bigger chunk of people's income and so has a deeper impact on those whose finances are already stretched, so the latest data on food prices is good news for many people.

One set of economists who will consider whether there is evidence of second-round effects are the nine people who set interest rates, which heavily influences the cost of borrowing money - such as mortgages - as well as the returns people get on savings.

The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee meets again in December and, after that, in February.

Having just raised interest rates - for the first time in more than three years - to 4%, there's a widespread expectation among analysts that another hike is to come.

To be clear, we don't know if and when that will happen for sure.

The case for an increase would be if prices continue to accelerate. The Bank will want to slow that down.

The case against would be price rises remaining relatively confined to energy-related costs. Any easing of Middle East tensions could limit price rises without Bank of England intervention.

As far as wages are concerned, the latest official data suggests that rising prices are largely covered by rising pay.

That is an average - so is not true for everyone - but how long it remains the case may be key to how deep upcoming price rises cut into our personal finances.

Business.title: Government backs welfare shake-up to prevent 'lost generation'
Business.text:
The government has backed plans by former minister Alan Milburn for sweeping reforms to prevent "losing a generation" of young people to a life on benefits.

Milburn proposes spending billions on tailored support for under 25s not in employment, education or training (Neets), to be part-funded by cuts to some benefits.

He claims his plan, which also proposes tax breaks for firms and major education reforms, will get 440,000 young people into jobs by 2036.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he endorsed the "principles" of the Milburn review and was confident he could persuade Labour MPs to back legislation to implement its measures.

The PM told Sky News he would set out a full response to the review next month, after he had received a separate report into Personal Independence Payments (Pips) by Social Security Minister Sir Stephen Timms.

But he added: "I have never in my years in politics seen a wholesale, whole government approach to supporting the next generation.

"That is what this represents, and I am absolutely confident that I can take this vision and get people behind it, indeed get the country behind it, because we will not place Britain in the position I want it to be in if we have a generation of young people growing up without hope for the future."

The government has made Milburn the head of a new new youth opportunities unit to deliver on his recommendations.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said her party agreed with Milburn's "diagnosis" but claimed Labour had "made the problem much worse for young people" by increasing employers' National Insurance contributions and the youth minimum wage.

There are few signs so far that Burnham will face a backlash from his own MPs of the scale that blocked his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer's planned £5bn welfare cuts last year.

But some left-wing Labour MPs and the Unison trade union have warned proposals to cut health-related benefits will drive some young people into poverty.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told MPs that "in future" the welfare state should be judged "not just by a snapshot of people's monthly incomes" but "but by the story of people's lives, and by their ability to achieve their full potential".

McFadden, who was flanked by Burnham and Chancellor John Healey during his statement in the Commons, said the government rejected claims that young people were "snowflakes and shirkers".

The million who were not in work or training had been robbed of the "prospect of a good future" and that was something that demanded "much more" than a conventional government response, he told MPs.

He said the government would publish draft proposals on welfare reform early next year, with legislation to follow.

In his wide-ranging 250 page report, external, Milburn proposes:

The report calls for the government to spend around £5.8bn in total by 2036-37 on extra mental health and employment support.

And it urges ministers to "kickstart the reform programme" next year, with an initial £500m, from "repriotising" existing spending.

Business.title: Speed camera fault may have allowed drivers to escape fines
Business.text:
Further problems with the accuracy of speed cameras on English roads have been uncovered which may have allowed drivers to slip through the cracks and escape fines.

National Highways discovered issues with speed cameras last year, affecting 154 out of 400 cameras but, following an investigation, said it had found another fault on units monitoring roads including those running between Huntingdon and Cambridge.

The Home Office has revoked approval that allows footage from the cameras to be used as evidence in legal proceedings. US firm Verra Mobility operates the cameras but National Highways said it will now end the contract.

Roads minister Justin Madders said: "We can't take chances with this.

"If we're going to prosecute people, we need to be confident the system is working as it should. That's why we've taken the action we have."

In a statement, Verra Mobility said it "remains fully committed to delivering reliable, innovative technology that helps make roads safer".

The fault affected all of the variable speed cameras on smart motorways, and a section of the A14 between Huntingdon and Cambridge as well as the A1 approach junction to the A14.

A spokesperson for National Highways said that Verra's camera system had been selected on the basis that it maintained Home Office approval.

The agency said that since that was no longer the case "we are ending our contractual relationship to use the cameras for enforcement".

It added: "We are considering all further commercial and legal options that may be appropriate."

The BBC has contacted Verra Mobility for comment.

Madders said that the enforcement of speed limits continues to be conducted through a range of different tactics, including mobile cameras as well as marked and unmarked police patrols.

But he admitted that the camera system will not be fully fixed until sometime next year.

Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at the RAC motoring organisation, said: "Malfunctioning speed cameras on smart motorways do more than just let speeding drivers get away with breaking the law and endangering lives – they further undermine confidence in the very types of road we know drivers already have serious misgivings about."

There are 4,000 cameras across the entire road network.

In December 2025, National Highways, which runs England's motorways, blamed an "anomaly" in how variable speed cameras were interacting with speed limit signs on some A roads and motorways.

For example, on a road where the speed limit increases, a driver may see a sign showing 60mph but the camera recording it may still be working on the basis of a previous 40mph speed limit.

The fault led to 2,650 wrongful speed camera activations between 2021 and the end of last year.

Those who had been wrongfully fined have been reimbursed.

As National Highways continued to test the system, it discovered a further problem "relating to how some of these cameras may activate in specific and rare circumstances".

It said that according to its calculations, "the circumstances in which the latest issue could occur are extremely rare, and there is no evidence to suggest it has impacted enforcement".

Nevertheless, it said it was "taking immediate steps to ensure compliance is maintained at relevant locations".

It said it would put further traffic officer patrols in place to monitor the sites.

Business.title: Waymo temporarily pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways
Business.text:
Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, the company has said.

The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless taxis from state freeways following a series of recent traffic incidents.

California's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) cited an "imminent hazard to public safety" for the ban, noting an incident this month in which several driverless Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101.

Waymo said it was working with state officials "diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations", adding that no injuries or collisions were reported following the incident on US Route 101 south of San Francisco.

California's DMV said Waymo's driverless taxis presented a risk "due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present".

In another incident earlier this month, footage widely seen on social media appeared to show a Waymo car trying to overtake patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing the pace of traffic on a San Francisco highway.

The California ban, which came into effect on 11 November, would remain in place until Waymo "demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions".

A Waymo spokesperson said: "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance."

Data on Waymo's website suggests that its cars, compared to human drivers, are involved in 95% fewer crashes resulting in serious injury.

Waymo currently operates driverless taxis in 15 US cities, but only offered freeway rides in a handful of those locations, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Miami.

The company's driverless taxis can continue to operate on regular city streets.

In May, Waymo recalled thousands of its self-driving cars in the US over a software issue that could allow vehicles to drive into flooded roads.

Business.title: British hacker who stole $11m jailed for six years in US
Business.text:
A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message phishing, and stealing more than $11.6m (£8.8m) in cryptocurrency from individual victims.

Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, started hacking as a teenager and was part of the collective of young hackers known as Scattered Spider, which has been blamed for a string of high profile cyber-crimes.

US prosecutors said the thefts had "severe, life-altering consequences" for victims and showed the growing threat posed by online crime groups.

The sentence brings to an end a years-long international investigation involving authorities in the UK, US, Spain and Canada.

Buchanan admitted taking part in a hacking campaign that began in 2021, when he was 19.

Working from his parents' home, he and other English-speaking hackers in the US and UK targeted employees at major technology and telecommunications companies.

It made them $8m in less than two years, according to US prosecutors.

Buchanan and his hacker gang sent out hundreds of SMS messages to the mobile phones of people who worked for large tech or telecoms companies.

The SMS phishing messages contained links to spoof websites designed to look like legitimate sites of victim companies.

The group used messages like "Hi, your account is due to expire - you need to log in to your work account here immediately or you will lose access to work apps".

The websites then lured the recipient into providing confidential information, including personal identifying information (PII), and account usernames and passwords.

The boys and young men did it on an industrial scale with Buchanan setting up a Telegram bot to collect all the victims' credentials as the duped workers unwittingly handed over their login details.

For some victim companies, subsequently stolen information included confidential work information, intellectual property, plus account access credentials, names, email addresses, and telephone numbers.

The group then used stolen information and SIM-swapping techniques to target cryptocurrency investors in the United States.

In the largest single theft, prosecutors said one victim lost $1.67m in December 2022.

Overall, authorities calculated that Buchanan and his co-conspirators stole more than $11.6m from victims.

Business.title: Judge extends deadline for Trump’s deposition in $10bn BBC lawsuit
Business.text:
Donald Trump has been granted a temporary delay before he must give a witness statement in his $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC.

In late October, Enjoliqué Lett, a federal magistrate judge, gave Trump a firm 11 December deadline to sit for a deposition by lawyers representing the BBC in his lawsuit against the British broadcaster. If he failed to do so by that date, he could be subject to penalties up to dismissal of the case, the judge warned.

But on Tuesday, the president got something of a reprieve when Jeffrey Kuntz, a federal district court judge, approved a joint motion by the parties and extended the deadline for Trump’s deposition until 22 January. The judge also pushed back the deadline for discovery in the case from 18 December to 29 January.

Trump had originally agreed to sit for a deposition on 16 October, but his team backed out, citing “matters of national importance”. That led the BBC to file a motion to compel Trump to sit for a deposition in a timely fashion.

According to the joint motion filed on Monday, the BBC has agreed to the Trump team’s proposal for the president to sit for a deposition between 11 January and 22 January after his representatives said he was unavailable to do so this year “due to his schedule and the nature of his profession”. As that timeline nears, the parties will meet to select a date and identify a secure location for the deposition.

“It is Trump’s case, so he should expect to be deposed,” Kuntz wrote in his order. “It appears he acknowledges that reality.”

The judge ordered the parties to schedule Trump’s deposition by Friday at noon. Kuntz scheduled a trial date for the case for 3 May 2027 in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.

So far, Trump’s lawyers have deposed seven defendant witnesses. As part of the agreement between Trump and the BBC, the president’s lawyers will not depose Samir Shah, the BBC chair, or a former BBC director-general – nor any current or former BBC employee – until the president sits for questioning.

While Trump’s seven-hour-long deposition will be videotaped, it will only be available to attorneys for the parties.

In addition to Trump, the BBC might also be able to depose his daughter, Ivanka Trump, his son, Donald Trump Jr, and his son-in-law Jared Kushner. “Defendant is currently conferring with President Trump and these non-parties regarding the subpoenas directed to them, given that these non-parties may be objecting to, or moving to quash, those subpoenas,” the parties wrote in their joint motion.

Last week, Kuntz, a Trump appointee, refused the BBC’s request to dismiss the case, though he threw out the president’s contention that the broadcaster violated Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by the BBC that spliced together two comments made nearly an hour apart by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot. The BBC has acknowledged that this specific edit was misleading, but Trump has gone on to claim, falsely, that the BBC did not just edit his speech but used AI to insert words into his speech.

“BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a 70-minute-long speech into 12 seconds,” the judge wrote in his ruling. “But the court is not persuaded.”

Business.title: Deutsche Bank dismissed warnings about dealings with risky clients, reports claim
Business.text:
Deutsche Bank reportedly dismissed warnings about its dealings with risky clients, including high-profile Russian oligarchs, to protect profits, the findings of an investigation into a trove of leaked bank documents indicate.

A leak of 15m internal files is reported to show that the troubled German bank repeatedly ignored concerns by its compliance officers about its risk-taking, despite having already been caught being used to launder billions of dollars for Russian criminals, spies and oligarchs between 2010 and 2015.

The investigations, which were published by media outlets including Der Spiegel, the Financial Times, the New York Times and Le Monde, will represent a fresh blow for Deutsche Bank, which has struggled to repair its reputation after a number of scandals and dealings with controversial clients including the US president, Donald Trump, and the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Deutsche Bank said on Tuesday that the issues raised in the investigations “date back many years, in some cases as much as two decades” and had been addressed by its leadership. “Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators.”

However, the reports suggested Deutsche Bank prioritised profit ahead of internal controls, and continued to expand its Russian business until 2021, despite warnings from internal compliance officers and growing geopolitical tensions between Nato allies and Moscow.

Deutsche Bank allegedly resisted pulling out of Russia even after the Kremlin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, before the bank did a U-turn and exiting the country in March that year.

The investigations suggested Deutsche Bank was driven by competitive pressure, including from American banks, and that its chief executive, Christian Sewing, pursued a growth strategy that involved doing business with a list of customers known as its “most sensitive clients”. That covered roughly 50 corporate clients ranked by how close they were to the Kremlin, and other potential risks including financial crime, according to the Financial Times.

Some names allegedly on that list included: Russia’s state-owned gas company Gazprom; petrochemicals group Sibur; and oligarchs including the aluminium magnate Oleg Deripaska, the report said.

Outside its Russian dealings, the German lender is facing fresh scrutiny for allegedly processing almost $600m (£454m) of suspicious payments linked to Epstein, much higher than previously known. Deutsche said it “regrets [its] historical relationship” with Epstein and that it had made “considerable investments in strengthening controls”.

The lender is also accused of accidentally leaking Trump’s tax documents to another client during his first term in office, which Deutsche Bank allegedly kept secret from the White House. Deutsche Bank said it did not comment on former or existing client relationships. Deutsche Bank cut ties with Trump in 2021.

The reports prompted a 4% drop in Deutsche Bank’s German-listed shares on Tuesday.

Deutsche Bank issued a public statement in response to the investigation on Tuesday, saying it had “gone through a fundamental transformation” under Sewing.

“We made substantial investments in our control environment while restoring sustainable profitability, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters. This involved €7bn of direct investments in our control environment between 2019 and 2025.”

The bank added: “We remain committed to ensuring continuous enhancements of our control environment and a culture of integrity and completing any outstanding remediation.”

“Regardless of how the information was obtained, it includes confidential information about clients, employees and other third parties, which remains legally protected. We have acted, and will continue to act, decisively to protect this,” the bank said.

Business.title: United Airlines says ‘widespread’ system outage resolved
Business.text:
United ⁠Airlines said on ⁠Monday ⁠that it had resolved ⁠a widespread system ⁠outage, just three days after the Federal ⁠Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop on all US flights.

“We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures. While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,” Chicago-based United said in a statement. “There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”

According to an internal memo from ​United’s pilots’ ‌union seen ‌by Reuters, a company-wide ‌web-based outage had affected multiple applications used by pilots, including crew communications. It said United was unable to provide final ‌aircraft weights for departing flights and advised pilots to ​follow airport station guidance on whether to leave their gates.

Before every departure, pilots use performance software, often on a cockpit tablet, to check that the aircraft can safely take off under current weather and runway conditions. The preflight calculations include the aircraft’s weight along with information about the fuel, baggage, cargo and passengers the plane is carrying.

Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said in an interview on Monday night that he did not know what caused the one-and-a-half-hour outage. “This is not ‌an FAA [Federal Aviation Administration] system-wide problem,” Duffy said on Fox News’s Hannity.

The United computer issue is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown to affect Americans in the last few days. On Friday, ageing equipment led to a temporary grounding of all commercial airplanes in the US for more than four hours, sparking travel chaos as thousands of flights were delayed or canceled.

Airlines have experienced similar disruptions before. ‌In August 2025, United temporarily grounded flights after a problem with its Unimatic system, which supplies flight information to systems used to calculate aircraft weight and balance. It was not immediately clear whether Monday’s outage ​involved United’s Unimatic system.

The Trump administration said the rare ground stop stemmed from a fiber upgrade during routine maintenance that led to data flooding, which crashed a critical communication system.

And earlier on Monday, customers reported service outages and difficulty accessing their online accounts at several major US banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.

It also comes after a major outage by Microsoft that began on Thursday and lasted into the next day, which crippled a host of services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. The outage had serious repercussions for millions of people and organizations all over the world, including schools, hospitals, businesses, courts, banks, prisons, police forces and governments.

Business.title: Americans relying on heating oil brace for harsh winter: ‘We’re often cold in our own home’
Business.text:
Millions of homeowners in the US will pay hundreds of dollars more this winter to heat their homes as rising energy prices have pushed up the price of heating oil.

The US Energy Information Administration projects households that use heating oil can expect to pay 21% more this year compared with last winter, with warmer temperatures expected to partly offset price increases.

About 3% of US households rely on heating oil as their primary heat source. In the winter of 2023-2024, 4.79m US households used heating oil as their primary heat source, 82% of which were households in the north-east.

A recent report from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association found that overall, heating costs are expected to climb over 7% nationwide, with average heating bills rising 16.9% in the north-east.

Residents in Maine, where the temperatures can reach below 0F in many parts of the state, said they are bracing themselves for a pricey winter.

“My home heating oil costs have doubled this year,” said Heidi Unruh, 61, of Kittery, Maine, where the winter chill comes in December and lasts through the end of March. “They were already impossibly high in Maine before Trump took office, and I will feel serious pain as the Maine weather dives to it’s typical winter chill”

It costs more than $1,500 to fill her 250-gallon tank at home, which has to be refilled every 47 days when the temperatures are low. The increase in costs has forced her to try to cut back on other expenses.

“Between oil prices, tariffs, and rising food and energy prices, it will be an especially difficult winter,” Unruh said. “Mainers everywhere will struggle along with me. To compensate, I grew a lot of my own food this year. I have cut back on unnecessary expenses, and am trying overall to need less.”

Nikki Papadopoulos, who lives in Piscataquis, a county in the central part of the state, said that her family has started to use a wood stove because the cost of propane has also been high. They have also cut back on hot water, trying to use cold water to wash dishes, as the water heater also uses oil.

“We keep our thermostat turned down to the absolute lowest setting available, and honestly, we’re often cold in our own home. We’re wearing layers, sweaters and jackets indoors just to stay warm,” Papadopoulos said. “We’ve cut out pretty much all unnecessary spending. We’re down to the bare essentials.”

Though her husband recently received a pay increase, it’s been nearly eaten up by the higher cost of heating.

“We’re essentially making compromises in our everyday routines just to stretch what’s in the tank,” she added. “We’re taking the hit from every direction.”

Around 50% of households in Maine relied on heating oil in 2024, a reliance that has declined in recent years, though Maine still has the highest proportion of homes using heating oil in the US.

“It’s a necessity. For people in colder regions of America, they need it, it’s what they keep themselves warm with,” said Justin Barnes, a fuel delivery driver in the Bangor, Maine region, who has had to give residents bills that have been much higher compared with recent years. “It seems like these politicians ain’t doing a lick to lower the prices or make our lives easier, which is their responsibility.”

Democrat Troy Jackson, a logger and former state senator, won his election against longtime Republican senator Susan Collins in the recent midterm elections, where Republicans across the country lost their races in what was largely seen as a repudiation against the rising cost of living.

Much of it has been driven by the war in Iran, where the closure of a key oil trading route has led to a prolonged spike in energy prices. Gas prices at the pump have risen over 30% compared with last year. Other oil products, such as diesel and heating oil, have gone up even higher. Recent data showed that heating oil saw a 74.2% increase from September 2025 to September 2026, costing over $6 a gallon on average.

Russia’s export ban on diesel, which is similar to heating oil, amid the country’s war with Ukraine has also affected energy prices, said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. In 2025, Russia exported 10% of internationally traded diesel.

The Trump administration has attempted to strike a deal with Russia to export some diesel to the US, but the effort has failed so far.

Bob Carpenter, an electrician in Greenville, Rhode Island, relies on heating oil to heat his home and has had to save up, bracing for the price hikes to refill his home’s oil tank. When his heating oil was delivered last month, it was $1,425 for roughly 240 gallons – about $600 more than he paid in previous years.

The higher cost of heating oil comes atop other bills that have gotten more expensive, including electricity bills. “Two years ago, I thought $250 was expensive. Lately, my bills have averaged around $350 a month, which is starting to feel like the new normal,” Carpenter said.

Carpenter said he’s concerned about the effect higher prices will have on the ability of younger generations, including his children, to save for emergencies.

“When necessities take up more of your budget, there’s less left for an unexpected car repair or a roof that needs replacing,” he added. “What concerns me goes beyond energy. It’s the combined cost of groceries, housing, insurance, and other necessities. Inflation means our money doesn’t stretch as far.”

Business.title: Several companies are using Trump tariff refunds for corporate bonuses
Business.text:
Several companies that received refunds for paying Donald Trump’s tariffs have put those funds towards corporate bonuses instead of reimbursing consumers, an investigation from ProPublica has found.

After analyzing securities filings and earnings calls, ProPublica identified at least nine companies who said they were receiving tariff refunds and noted they were directing some of those funds to their leadership.

Stanley Black & Decker, a tool company that makes common household products including vacuums, electric drills and measuring tapes, told its consumers they were forced to raise prices because of Trump’s import fees, ProPublica reported. The company is expected to receive at least $298m in tariff reimbursements and indicated some of it will go to bonuses. Executives at TJ Maxx and Marshalls, discount department stores that are set to receive tariff refunds, also said the same.

A spokesperson for TJ Maxx and Marshalls, which are owned by the same TJX parent company, confirmed ProPublica’s reporting, and said that the company received an aggregate of $331m in refunds for a portion of the tariffs covered in the supreme court ruling. Because of these refunds, the company now had accrued “incremental expenses of $112 million for year-end incentive compensation and discretionary bonuses for eligible associates globally”, the spokesperson said.

“Given that this is an accrual, and we have not reached the end of our current fiscal year, we have not disclosed any breakout beyond this,” the company spokesperson said.

In financial disclosures, Stanley Black & Decker said the refund it received “was partially offset by directly attributable costs for variable incentive compensation”, according to ProPublica. Stanley Black & Decker did not immediately respond to request for comment.

The Trump administration has refunded at least $100bn to companies since August, about 60% of roughly $165bn in tariffs, after the supreme court ruled that Trump’s “liberation day” tariffs were illegal. The court ruled that the tariffs were unlawful because they overstepped his executive authority and should have required congressional approval.

Some companies immediately sued the US government for refunds after the ruling, though Trump signaled that he would “remember” which companies requested reimbursements and praised companies for holding off. The Trump administration has not specified which companies are receiving refunds, despite requests for information, according to ProPublica.

Though many companies said publicly that they had to increase prices because of tariffs, it has largely been unclear what companies are doing with their tariff refunds.

In its analysis, ProPublica found that almost all the companies that have publicly said they plan to use their tariff reimbursements to refund customers are those that deal directly with other businesses, rather than directly consumers. Some companies have remained “vague” about their plans for the reimbursements and have not specified whether those funds will go towards price decreases or holding back on future increases, according to the report.

Research has shown that US consumers have shouldered some of the cost of tariffs, with the New York Federal Reserve estimating that 26% of tariff increases pass through to consumer prices. The Yale Budget Lab estimated that tariffs cost households about $900 annually under current laws.

Tariffs are one of several of Trump’s economic policies that have proven unpopular with voters, reflected in the widespread victories Democrats notched in the November midterms. A year after Trump’s tariffs were announced, a survey from the Pew Research Center found that 63% of Americans felt little or no confidence in his handling of tariffs.

Republican candidates across the country were largely punished for Trump’s tariffs and other White House decisions that have led to greater inflation. In the Associated Press’s November survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters, two-thirds said that Trump’s decisions had fueled inflation, while about half of 2022 midterm voters said the same thing about former president Joe Biden’s policies.
