Business.title: Trump backs calls for reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO
Business.text:
Donald Trump has expressed support for the return of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, joining Silicon Valley heavyweights in backing the reinstatement of the AI figurehead.

The US president referred to a tech industry campaign for Huang’s rehabilitation, saying a “big group” of people would like him back.

“I think he learned a big lesson. I guess maybe one lesson is more important than ⁠another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump told ​reporters as he left the ‌White House on ‌a trip to Asia. “He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return.”

The comments came as the US government announced a crackdown on companies such as Nvidia selling AI chips and servers to overseas datacentres that in turn are supplying computing power to China and other US adversaries.

Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, and a host of other tech bosses have signed an open letter calling for the reinstatement of Huang.

The reinstatement letter has more than 165,000 signatories and demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.

The former Nvidia CEO resigned last Thursday amid reports of extramarital liaisons, including with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who is no relation. His resignation ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded.

Days earlier, Huang had admitted being unfaithful to his wife without specifying who else was involved.

Trump said on Monday: “Nobody’s proven that [Alice Huang] is a spy. She may not be a spy.” Trump has faced questions after it was reported that a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in his administration.

According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed with people close to him a possible return to the company. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for his return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House. The FT also reported on Monday that Nvidia’s board was not considering reinstating Huang.

One analyst downplayed the prospect of a Huang return, describing the notion of the ex-CEO’s reinstatement as “ridiculous”. Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the range of issues facing Huang and Nvidia, from personal conduct to questions over China, made an external candidate or the permanent appointment of the interim CEO – Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer – the best option.

“We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO, and for the company the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette,” he said, describing the petition as “noise and distraction”.

The new rule announced by the US government on Monday requires companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on ⁠them being illegally diverted.

“The rule ‌is designed to ​ensure that ​existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving datacentres in third countries,” the US Department of Commerce said.

Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy, worked as an executive at the Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. According to reports, Megaspeed is under suspicion of diverting powerful Nvidia chips to China in contravention of US export laws.

Megaspeed said on Sunday it was a “legitimate and lawful business” and that Huang had left the business in late 2025. It added that it complied “with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate”.

Nvidia shares closed down 4.1% on Monday, knocking about $160bn (£121bn) off Nvidia’s market capitalisation, lowering it to $3.76tn compared with $4.5tn before the scandal broke.

Sports.title: Sandpapergate: Cummins, Bancroft, Lehmann, Warner - who said what about Australia scandal?
Sports.text:
The sandpaper scandal, one of the biggest controversies in the history of Test cricket, continues to engulf Australian sport.

Fresh evidence from Cameron Bancroft - the culprit of the ball-tampering in South Africa in 2018 - has heaped pressure on Australia captain Pat Cummins, former coach Darren Lehmann and Cricket Australia.

In a detailed account of more than 4,000 words published in the West Australian newspaper, Bancroft alleges all the Australia players and coaches present in Cape Town eight years ago knew of the plot.

Bancroft's explosive testimony supports claims made by Usman Khawaja, David Warner and Chadd Sayers.

However, Cummins denied Khawaja's version of events in his own extraordinary news conference in Sydney last week. Cummins spoke to the media for 68 minutes in an address broadcast on live television.

Here, BBC Sport collects the most recent accounts of players and coaches involved in the saga that became widely known as sandpapergate.

Batter Khawaja played all four Tests in South Africa and a total of 88 for Australia before retiring from international cricket earlier this year.

Revelations in his autobiography reignited debate around the sandpaper scandal and made headlines across the globe.

"It was all of us," Khawaja said. "Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.

"In an ideal world, I don't want to do this. I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now.

"Even in the change rooms when I was talking to them after the game. I said, 'Take this as a team'.

"We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team, and so I was always of that stance."

Warner was Australia's opening batter and vice-captain during the 2018 series. He, along with captain Steve Smith and Bancroft, were the three players punished for the ball-tampering.

The Cricket Australia (CA) investigation in 2018 found Warner developed the plan and that he instructed Bancroft to carry out the cheating.

After serving his ban, Warner returned to play a further 133 times for Australia across formats, including three Ashes series and the 2023 World Cup win. He retired from international cricket in 2024.

In response to Khawaja's book, Warner said: "I thank you for what you've done. It's 100% accurate what you've said. Now everyone knows the truth."

He also accused Cricket Australia of a cover-up, describing the CA investigation as "rushed" and botched".

"As far as l am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," Warner said.

"If that's correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?"

The Cape Town Test was the 13th of Cummins' Test career. A key bowler, he would go on to be named Australia's Test captain in 2021. It is a position he still holds.

Prior to Khawaja's book, Cummins and the other bowlers from Cape Town - Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon - had always denied knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper.

In an extraordinary news conference last week, Cummins called Khawaja's claims that the whole team knew about the plan "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense".

"I said that consistently for the last eight years," Cummins said. "I did not know that was happening.

"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."

Asked if he knew of any plans at any stage to tamper with the ball during the series against South Africa, Cummins said: "No."

Cummins also said he did not remember a meeting where Khawaja had called on the team to take collective responsibility - something his former team-mate claimed.

Opening batter Bancroft was playing his eighth Test in Cape Town, aged 25. He was the player caught using sandpaper on the field.

He played another two Tests after serving his ban and is still playing for Western Australia. He turns 34 this week.

In 2021, Bancroft said it was "self-explanatory" whether the bowlers knew of the plan, and on Wednesday he backed Khawaja's account, saying Cummins' news conference made him "feel angry, betrayed and alone".

Like Khawaja, Bancroft said sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa – the match before he was caught - and also said he had conversations with the Australia seamers about whether the ball was "swinging enough".

He said the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaper. He also claimed that coach Lehmann and bowling coach David Saker were present in the initial discussions and that Bancroft's role was also discussed in a team meeting before day three.

In an account published by the West Australian on Wednesday, Bancroft wrote: "All the bowlers gave me feedback if my work on the ball was working. It was helpful.

"Is it going yet? It's not going yet, it needs more. So I would use the sandpaper more on the ball.

"There was even a time I was told to stop out of fear what I was doing was becoming too obvious."

Lehmann was Australia coach at the time of the scandal. He was cleared by the CA investigation and said he had "no prior knowledge" of the plan to ball-tamper.

He resigned after the series and has been Northamptonshire coach since the start of the 2025 English season.

After Khawaja's revelations, Lehmann said: "I don't think everyone would have known [about the use of sandpaper]. You do know ball-tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years."

After Cricket Australia said it would hold an open forum, Lehmann said he has "nothing to hide".

Speaking on radio coverage of the third one-day international against England after Bancroft's account was published, Lehmann said: "I need to sit back, process it and work through each allegation.

"That's what I'll be doing over the next few days.

"I need to have a really good read of it. I need to make sure I'm saying what I want to say."

Smith, one of the greatest batters of his generation, was Australia's captain at the time of the scandal.

After serving a 12-month ban, he returned for the World Cup and Ashes the following year and has stood in as captain at times since.

He was found to have been aware of the plan to cheat and to mislead the public and match officials.

Smith, who broke down in tears when apologising at a subsequent news conference, as cameras captured the emotional toll of the moment, has not spoken publicly since Khawaja's book was published.

Speaking about the episode in September this year, he said: "That was a traumatic experience in my life and when I hear the flash of a camera it makes me revisit that in a way.

"I've tried to kind of erase a lot of 2018 and what happened. I can't remember a lot about the series. I've tried to block most of it out of my memory bank."

Marsh was bowling when Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball in Cape Town. As an all-rounder, he was not part of the 2021 bowlers' statement.

Marsh was captain during Australia's recent ODI series against England and refused to answer questions on the topic before the series opener.

"I am not here to share mine [story] today," he said.

"I respect Uzzie [Khawaja] has told his story; my focus is on tomorrow. I am not here to go back on South Africa."

Following the conclusion of the series, Marsh did not take part in his post-match news conference, with 26-year-old bowler Jack Edwards taking his place.

Paine was Australia's wicketkeeper during the South Africa series and was made captain when Smith was banned.

He served in the role until he stood down in 2021 over a historical investigation into sexually explicit text messages sent to a female colleague.

In his autobiography, Paine said the suggestion everyone in the Australia dressing room must have known about the sandpaper use is "rubbish" and claimed he first found out when images appeared on the big screen in Cape Town.

"Everyone out there was shocked when they looked up on the big screen and saw Cameron Bancroft with a piece of sandpaper in his hand," Paine wrote. "I was stunned. We all were.

"My heart sank, I was thinking, 'What the f***?' A sense of dread came over us all."

Bancroft said he discussed whether the ball was reversing with Paine during the second Test.

Saker was Australia's bowling coach during the South Africa series.

Bancroft alleged Saker was present for discussions about the use of sandpaper and told the batter he needed to do more to the ball.

Saker was also England bowling coach as recently as last month's tri-series in Pakistan. He was an influential part of England's 2010-11 Ashes win.

In 2021, reflecting on the sandpaper saga, Saker said: "Obviously a lot of things went wrong at that time. There was a lot of people to blame. It could have been me to blame, it could have been someone else. It could have been stopped and it wasn't, which is unfortunate.

"Cameron's a very nice guy. He's just doing it to get something off his chest… He's not going to be the last. You could point your finger at me, you could point your finger at Boof [Lehmann]. Could you point it at other people? Of course you could.

"The disappointing thing is it's never going to go away. Regardless of what's said. We all know that we made a monumental mistake. The gravity wasn't as plain until it all came out."

Starc was an integral part of the vaunted Australia attack in Cape Town and remains so in the present day. He is ranked as the number one bowler in Test cricket by the International Cricket Council.

Left-armer Starc repeatedly denied knowledge of the sandpaper plot, including in the statement released with Cummins, Hazlewood and Lyon in 2021, and in a news conference in the days after Khawaja's claims emerged.

Speaking on 10 November, Starc said: "Obviously, there's differing opinions of eight years ago. We were heavily grilled through the process at the time, and since, and I guess I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers, but where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed. My recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021.

"I'll stick to what I said five years ago, what I said at the time, eight years ago. Clearly, there's different versions from different people, and I'll leave it where I left it back then."

A swing bowler, Sayers played his only Test for Australia after the sandpaper controversy erupted – the fourth and final match of the series against South Africa in Johannesburg.

Sayers, who retired from first-class cricket in 2021, spoke to Australian radio station SEN in the aftermath of Khawaja's claims, to corroborate the former batter's account.

Sayers claimed to have removed sandpaper from the field in the second Test against South Africa, the match before Bancroft was caught. He also backed up Khawaja's assertion that the entire Australia squad discussed the sandpaper issue after it was revealed in Cape Town.

Speaking on 15 November, Sayers said: "I am comfortable sitting here that I believe everyone in that side knew what was going on and what was being used.

"It was used in two Test matches and there were discussions in the changing rooms.

"After the occurrence in Cape Town, we all sat in the changing rooms after that day's play and, probably for 60 to 90 minutes, we talked about what had happened and I guess where to next."

Spinner Holland, who retired in 2021, was also a back-up bowler on the trip.

He also said there was a meeting held in the fallout from Cape Town about players taking responsibility.

"Once we got back to the hotel we did sit as a group [to discuss] what had happened and who was going to take the blame," Holland told newspaper The Australian.

"To Davey's [Warner's] credit, from what I remember, he did put his hand up and say he would take some of the responsibility, but not all of it.

"To be sitting there and seeing three blokes hung out to dry when you are supposed to be part of a team was a pretty hard watch."

Batter Handscomb was Australia's 12th man on the day Bancroft was caught, making frequent trips between the field and the dressing room.

Bancroft's account alleges Handscomb was told by Lehmann, via walkie-talkie, to "get the sandpaper off Bangers [Bancroft] now".

Last week, following Khawaja's claims but before Bancroft spoke, Handscomb was asked for his recollections after making a century for Victoria in the Sheffield Shield against Western Australia.

On 11 November, Handscomb said: "I appreciate you have to ask these questions. I've had a nice day today, it's not really something that I want to comment on right now. I'll sort of just let the powers of be do their thing."

Former England batter Hick was part of the Australia backroom team on the South Africa tour of 2018.

Hick was made redundant by Cricket Australia as part of a series of cost-cutting measures in 2020.

Speaking to the Sydney Morning Herald last week, Hick said: "I have seen the various statements around the coaches, and I'm very disappointed with the broad nature of them.

"Khawaja puts it simply: 'It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us'. To me, what Khawaja is implying here is absolutely false.

"In regard to any discussions around the ball-tampering in Port Elizabeth or Cape Town, I will say in true honesty that I did not hear or know anything.

"My first knowledge of all this was, like many, when it appeared on the big screen in Cape Town as I was sat on the outside balcony at the time."

Sports.title: The tightest Premier League survival scrap for years? Why it's not too early to worry for Man Utd, Sunderland and Crystal Palace
Sports.text:
Despite being only 10 games into the season, sitting in the relegation zone even at this early stage is more worrying than you might think.

But with how tight the Premier League table is, this could also be one of the fiercest relegation battles we have seen in a long time.

Two of the current bottom three, Crystal Palace and Manchester United, will resume their campaigns at the weekend with new managers after appointing Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino respectively.

Sunderland, wedged between the pair in 19th, have not pressed the panic button and have kept faith with Regis le Bris.

But is it too early to worry? We look at what the stats tell us about relegation battles in the past and what we can learn for the months ahead.

Looking at every Premier League season since it changed to a 20-team league in 1995-96, the current bottom three have cause to be concerned.

In 19 of the previous 31 seasons (61%), only one of the bottom three sides after 10 games managed to avoid relegation.

For fairness and accuracy, the 'bottom three' are the three sides with the worst record after 10 games, not simply those in the relegation zone after matchweek 10, since in some seasons a team had played nine games by that point.

Only in 10 seasons (32%) have two or more of the bottom three stayed up - and that has not happened in any of the past eight campaigns. The last time more than one team avoided the drop was in 2017-18, when all three survived.

That has only happened twice, although only twice have all three sides been relegated.

Overall, of the 93 previous teams in the bottom three after 10 games, 41 survived and 52 were relegated - a survival rate of 44%.

This is the third time that Palace have been bottom after 10 games. On both previous occasions, they did not just survive but thrived, finishing 11th.

They did so under Tony Pulis in 2013-14 and under Roy Hodgson in 2017-18. Both managers, like Frank, were appointed early in the season following poor starts under Ian Holloway and Frank de Boer respectively.

The 2013-14 season is the only previous time that Sunderland and Palace were the bottom two at this stage. The Black Cats also survived thanks to a great, late escape under Gus Poyet.

This is the first time United have been in the bottom three after 10 games of a Premier League season.

Given the size and resources of the club, it is unlikely they will go down, although the team in 18th place at this stage have been relegated in each of the past six seasons.

Fans of all three clubs will hope for a repeat of 2017-18, when not only Palace but the bottom three improved significantly to finish comfortably mid-table.

Sunderland's eight points is also the most that a side in 19th place have had for 16 years. Wolves had nine points in 2010-11 and survived in 17th.

In fact, only five points separate the bottom half of the Premier League, with Tottenham in 11th on 12 points and Palace bottom with seven – the smallest gap at this stage for 24 years.

The highest that a team in the bottom three after 10 games have finished the season is eighth - Bolton in 2003-04, Tottenham in 2008-09 and Everton in 2017-18 - which suggests it will be Conference League at best for Manchester United next season.

Then again, the table is so tight that only nine points separate Chelsea in fifth and Palace - the smallest gap at this stage for 16 years.

Given that fifth place has been enough to qualify for the Champions League in recent seasons, optimistic United fans may not be ruling it out just yet.

As mentioned, this season has both the 'best' bottom side in terms of points and the most compact bottom half of the table that we have seen at this stage since 2002-03.

In that season, West Ham were relegated on the final day with 42 points - the most a side have been relegated with in Premier League history.

Given the way this season is shaping up, 40 points might also not be enough to survive.

Sports.title: Rassie Erasmus: South Africa's maverick coach plans online watchalong
Sports.text:
Having been banned from the touchline for six matches, you will not find Rassie Erasmus at the Aviva Stadium when his South Africa side face Ireland.

Instead he will be hosting an online watchalong of Saturday's match, courtesy of a swiftly purchased domain name.

The South Africa head coach plans to stream his reactions live while watching on television from his team's Dublin hotel.

It is typical Erasmus. An unapologetic, unabashed show of defiance in the face of the authorities.

And he will not be short of virtual company.

Because, while Erasmus has run low of advocates elsewhere, his compatriots have rushed to his defence.

"Rassie was just asking questions," said former South Africa hooker Hanyani Shimange in the wake of Erasmus' ban for a scattergun series of complaints about the injustices suffered by his side.

"But you have to look at the facts. Where was the accountability for that refereeing performance [in the loss to France]?"

Naas Botha, legendary South Africa fly-half turned pundit, described Erasmus' punishment as a "debacle". "You can't tell me [officials] are untouchable," he said.

Supersport, which broadcasts South Africa's games domestically, published an article accusing Erasmus' critics of "pearl clutching", external and "shooting the messenger" with regards to the game's faults.

Despite slurring officials with a suggestion of match-fixing, Erasmus has the support of South Africa.

It is not surprising.

His feats with the team are astonishing.

South Africa were ranked sixth in the world when he took over in March 2018.

He arrived after a November tour in which they lost to Wales and were thrashed 38-3 by Ireland. New Zealand had racked up a record 57-0 win a few months earlier.

Erasmus turned the team around at speed, marrying their trademark up-front power with pace out wide.

They won the 2019 World Cup. The defended their title in 2023. They will go into the tournament in 2027 aiming for an unprecedented hat-trick. And few would bet against them achieving it.

Erasmus is relentlessly innovative.

Long before the sport's data revolution, he was coding game footage, picking up the technique from a friend who worked in the military. He has since developed Outfox, his own software which allows his teams to run through moves virtually on a screen away from the pitch.

Tactically, he has also been ahead of the curve. He pioneered the use of forward-heavy replacement benches, giving his team an edge in the final quarter of the match.

He saw the game-breaking potential of diminutive Sevens specialist Kurt-Lee Arendse and moulded Andre Esterhuizen into a genuine hybrid player, capable of playing in the back row and the backline.

Trick plays - forcing a scrum with a deliberate infringement off kick-off, or setting up a line-out in the middle of the pitch - have been part of Erasmus' arsenal.

Legally, he is across every possible loophole.

There was controversy before the match against France last weekend when he made use of the Nations Championships' looser regulations to swap his starting front row just over an hour before kick-off.

Previously, he demoted himself to water boy so he could run the touchline during the 2021 series win over the British and Irish Lions.

Former Springbok wing Bryan Habana worked under Erasmus at the Stormers in Cape Town.

"He is one of the master tacticians the game has ever seen," Habana told BBC Sport's Ireland Rugby Social.

"I don't always agree with how Rassie comes across, but I understand he wears his heart on his sleeve. He has got incredibly high standards.

"He's willing to be in the firing line to defend what he believes is right."

But there is no doubt, by the letter of the law, that Erasmus is wrong - certainly in terms of the platform and terms he chose for his complaints.

In July World Rugby introduced new rules around criticism of officials. It specifically targeted "comments which, viewed objectively, a reasonable person would conclude were an attack on the credibility or competence of the match officials".

Mentioning "match-fixing" undermines the officials in exactly that way.

Considering Erasmus' previous, including an hour-long monologue bemoaning officiating of a first-Test defeat by the Lions in 2021 and a series of tweets after a loss to France a year later, he may be fortunate to only be banned for six matches.

World Rugby, perhaps pre-empting the reaction in South Africa, was clear that it was not punishing Erasmus for asking questions.

"Robust, respectful debate is natural, but teams have access to well-established and supported channels and protocols for raising officiating matters before and after matches," it said in its judgement.

"Challenging a decision is not the same as questioning an official's integrity or making comments that expose them to personal abuse."

For many South Africans, though, Erasmus is still an outlaw hero.

World Rugby, based in Dublin, is seen by them as tilted towards the north.

Australian Brett Robinson, the current chairman, is the first figure from outside the Six Nations countries to hold the organisation's top job since it became an elected position.

The World Cup has been lifted by South Africa on four occasions, but held there only once.

Japan coach Eddie Jones, Erasmus' fellow maverick, recently suggested Ireland's political clout, external was behind his team's home game being staged in Australia rather than Tokyo.

South Africa were a powerful voice against the possible moves to "depower" the scrum - a key part of the Springbok game - at a February conference to discuss future law tweaks.

Erasmus' public pronouncements have fuelled conspiracy theories weaved from those threads. They have also made an all-time great team harder for outsiders to love.

Whether it is a deliberate ploy is hard to tell.

Certainly Erasmus is a repeat offender, but his offences have also come in his second language. He is an Afrikaans speaker.

Some also see instinctive honesty rather than a premeditated ploy in his public speaking.

"He also has almost no filters, so he will speak his mind without fully appreciating the consequences of what he has done," his biographer David O'Sullivan told BBC Sport in 2023.

Whatever the motivation, the consequences keep coming - for Erasmus, but also the rest of world rugby.

Referees Nic Berry and Wayne Barnes, previous targets of Erasmus' criticism, have detailed the effects it had on them.

Berry described "a character assassination" that caused "immeasurable damage". He has not refereed a South Africa game in the five years since.

Barnes' wife and children were threatened over social media.

South Africa's latest appeal to their supporters not to abuse officials, external may be too late for referee Andrea Piardi and his television match official Matteo Liperini, who oversaw France's win on Friday.

There is a wider question too.

For a complex sport, the image of a world champion coach publicly criticising officials does not little to dispel a wavering viewer's assumption that it is too intricate and confusing to justify their attention.

South Africa will always line up alongside their rebel chief.

But the patience of the rest of the rugby world with Erasmus' antics is wearing ever thinner.

Sports.title: Joint-record six referee errors in last Premier League weekend
Sports.text:
The Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel has ruled there were six on-field errors in the last round of games - the joint-highest it has recorded in one weekend.

Each week, the five members of the panel assess all the contentious incidents and vote whether both the referee and the video assistant referee (VAR) have got the decisions correct.

You have to go back to the early part of the 2023-24 season to find the last time there were six mistakes logged.

The statistic does not include correct VAR interventions to fix errors, such as the red card shown to Brentford's Igor Thiago.

In the last round of games almost every fixture had a contentious refereeing situation which was hotly debated.

It started on Friday with a potential penalty to Coventry City for a hair pull by Everton's James Tarkowski.

Arsenal were denied a penalty following a VAR review after it was deemed Kai Havertz was offside.

Tottenham lodged a complaint over a challenge by Leeds United's Jayden Bogle, who was not shown a red card.

And Liverpool argued against a late Crystal Palace penalty.

But which decisions did the KMI Panel rule were incorrect? Some of the votes might surprise you.

Such was the controversy across the weekend, it may come as a surprise that the KMI Panel ruled only two were missed VAR interventions. There have been six missed overall, the same number as this stage last season.

Incident 1: Coventry's Caleb Yirenkyi appeared to have his hair pulled inside the area by Everton's James Tarkowski. No penalty was awarded.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 incorrect, for the on-field decision and the VAR.

What the KMI Panel said: "Tarkowski had a hold of Yirenkyi's hair and the panel unanimously felt that VAR should have intervened."

Incident 2: Arsenal's Kai Havertz was pulled down inside the area by Hull City's Nobel Mendy. The VAR, Michael Oliver, sent referee Farai Hallam to the pitchside monitor but it was not given due to an offside offence by the Germany international.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 incorrect, for the on-field decision and the VAR.

What the KMI Panel said: "Although Harvertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence."

When the KMI Panel sits down to vote there are two separate considerations.

The first is on the decision of the referee, which is a basic judgement in law and the Premier League's expected interpretation.

The second is on the potential VAR intervention. This takes into account what the referee has said, the available replay angles and the high bar for intervention.

Incident 1: Thierno Barry put Everton in front against Coventry in the 61st minute, but there was a VAR check for a potential handball.

KMI Panel vote: 2:3 incorrect on the field, but 5:0 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "On the balance of probability the ball did accidentally strike Barry's hand. However, the readily available footage did not provide conclusive evidence."

Incident 2: Crystal Palace were awarded a penalty against Liverpool three minutes into stoppage time for a foul by Milos Kerkez on Dario Osorio. But was it just a clash of heads?

KMI Panel vote: 0:5 incorrect on the field, but 5:0 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "A penalty was incorrect with the contact being inevitable. However, it was not a clear and obvious error."

Incident 3: Ipswich were awarded a 72nd-minute penalty against Bournemouth for a foul by Lewis Cook on Abdoul Ouattara.

KMI Panel vote: 1:4 incorrect on the field, but 4:1 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "Ouattara made a clear step across Cook who didn't make a challenge and the referee's decision to award a penalty was incorrect. However, it was not a clear and obvious error."

Incident 4: Potential second yellow card for Bournemouth's Marcus Tavernier.

KMI Panel vote: 2:3 incorrect on the field; no VAR intervention possible.

What the KMI Panel said: "There was a clear, deliberate action by Tavernier to delay the restart."

Some of the most high-profile decisions from across the weekend have not yet featured.

That is because they have been voted to be correct on the field and through VAR.

Incident 1: Leeds United's Jayden Bogle caught Tottenham's Mathys Tel on high on his ankle. There was no VAR review for a red card.

KMI Panel vote: 3:2 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "The majority felt Bogle was looking to challenge with his right leg and his left leg came down on the back of Tel's ankle without the speed, force or intensity to be serious foul play. Two panellists felt that the challenge was sufficiently dangerous to merit a red card."

Incident 2: Chelsea's Cole Palmer went down on the edge of the area under a challenge by Sunderland's Luke O'Nien.

KMI Panel vote: 4:1 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "Clear contact made by O'Nien on Palmer which the panel felt should have been penalised with a free-kick on the basis that contact was made outside the area. One panellist felt that the foul contact was inside the area."

Incident 3: Sunderland were awarded a penalty when Levi Colwill was ruled to have tripped Brian Bobbey.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "There was upper body holding from both players as they progressed into the penalty area before a careless trip by the Chelsea defender."

Incident 4: Possible foul by Senne Lammens on Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki before Patrick Dorgu's 96th-minute equaliser.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "Although Lammens turned away from the ball, the contact he made on Suzuki was not impactful."

The KMI Panel was scrapped this summer in the Scottish Premiership because clubs became frustrated with the voting patterns of its members.

But it is more important in the Premier League, with the results creating a merit table which contributes to 50% of referees' salaries in bonus payments.

Many fans will feel there should have been more than two VAR errors logged in the last round of games.

Yet the KMI Panel does not exist to mirror the opinion of supporters.

Crucially, it uses the laws of the game and how the Premier League expects its games to be refereed as the barometer.

Still, six on-field mistakes - plus the Thiago red card - is clearly a high number.

And fans struggle to understand why it seems to be OK to have these on-field errors, and not correct them due to the high bar.

It all adds to the frustration of VAR.

Sports.title: ATP Finals: Carlos Alcaraz outclasses Daniil Medvedev despite injury concern
Sports.text:
Carlos Alcaraz continued his sensational late-season form as he outclassed world number five Daniil Medvedev to all but confirm his progress at the ATP Finals.

But the 23-year-old Spaniard later said he had felt "a little problem" with his hamstring.

Alcaraz produced another sparkling display to control the contest throughout, despite ending the match with heavy strapping on his upper-left leg.

The issue did not disrupt the world number three, who led by a set and a break when he received treatment on the area, as he cruised to a 6-2 6-4 win in just 72 minutes.

"Right now I'm just feeling OK," Alcaraz said.

"We will see with my team and physio, but I think the rest of today and tomorrow are really going to be important days ahead of me."

It was an 11th consecutive victory for the seven-time major winner, following back-to-back titles at the Vienna Open and Paris Masters.

Alcaraz will qualify for the semi-finals before his last group match against Flavio Cobolli on Friday if Frances Tiafoe wins a set against the Italian later on Wednesday.

Asked what pleased him most about his performance, Alcaraz replied: "Everything".

"We could see in [Medvedev's] first match that he was serving very well. I returned really well, really aggressively, and really deep," he added.

"I think I just hit the ball in a sweet spot every time. I'm really happy about it."

Given the outstanding levels at which he is currently operating, it is easy to forget that Alcaraz spent four months out of action in the middle of the season.

The former world number one's rapid return from that wrist injury to his scintillating best has been astonishing.

Alcaraz has won three titles and lost just twice in 24 matches since making his return at the US Open in August, when his lack of match fitness appeared to catch up with him in a four-and-a-half hour epic against Ben Shelton.

Just 10 weeks on, he delivered one of the best indoor performances of his career in sweeping past 2020 champion Medvedev.

That came two days after he began his latest bid for a first ATP Finals title with a statement victory over Tiafoe - and later warned his rivals he has never felt better at this stage of the season.

Medvedev beat home hope Cobolli in straight sets in his opening match for his first win against a top-10 opponent since defeating Alcaraz at Indian Wells in March.

The Russian was no match for the Australian Open champion on this occasion, however.

A dominant seven-game streak ultimately decided the match, as Alcaraz ran away with the first set and then broke immediately in the second to take firm control.

The second seed did not face a single break point as he outmanoeuvred Medvedev, firing 16 winners and committing just 13 unforced errors.

It was a display which scored 9.5 out of 10 on the ATP's performance rating, which combines several statistics to measure a player's overall game, following a 9.6 in his opener.

That was despite Alcaraz playing the final seven games with the issue in his hamstring, which he will now work to overcome in the next 48 hours.

Sports.title: England in Australia: Harry Brook's side win decider for statement series win
Sports.text:
Third one-day international, Hobart

England 328 (48.3 overs): Duckett 133, Jacks 59; Edwards 4-31

Australia 231 (46.5 overs): Renshaw 55; Baker 4-45

England won by 97 runs

England confidently swept aside Australia in the third one-day international in Hobart to seal a statement series win.

At times the series decider felt inconsequential - the latest seismic turn in Australia's sandpaper scandal taking all attention during Australia's chase - but Harry Brook's side won by 97 runs in an important step as they build towards next year's World Cup.

Even when failing to fully take advantage of a fast start, England reached 328 before being bowled out in the penultimate over, with Ben Duckett making a fine 133 from 115 balls.

Duckett's century, after all of his struggles in last winter's Ashes, was his first for England on Australian soil. A 48-ball 59 from Will Jacks ensured his innings was not wasted as Australia's spinners slowed scoring through the middle.

Just as impressive was another exciting effort from England's new-ball pair Gus Atkinson and Sonny Baker.

Atkinson dismissed Travis Head for the third time in a row in the first over - something to be noted before next year's Ashes series. He also hit Cameron Green with a brutal bouncer that forced the all-rounder to retire hurt.

Baker had Australia captain Mitchell Marsh caught at second slip in the second over, soon added the wicket of Josh Inglis and also dismissed Green's concussion replacement Oliver Peake en route to figures of 4-45.

It helped England calmly close out the win and, after being dismissed for 131 in the series opener, their recovery is noteworthy.

Australia, meanwhile, have questions to ponder on and off the field - many of which are unlikely to be answered before a five-match T20 series begins between these sides on Saturday.

On the field, Australia can at least point to the fact key bowlers – most notably under-fire captain Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood – have been rested for this series as a caveat for their defeat.

On the evidence of this series, England, though inconsistent, look the more settled side.

England had taken strides in ODI cricket this year, beating Sri Lanka (twice) and India, only to be checked by their horror defeats in Pakistan last month. This corrects that course.

Duckett was impressive again but the most significant learning from this series may be the emergence of Baker in partnership with Atkinson.

The 23-year-old Hampshire quick was brought in after defeat in the first ODI and has added real threat with the new ball in his first meeting with Australia.

Bowling has been England's weaker suit in recent ODIs but, given another good start, Liam Dawson was again able to ease through his overs of left-arm spin, bowling Cooper Connolly, having Jack Edwards caught at short fine leg and taking Matt Renshaw caught and bowled with his second ball.

Dropped chances – Baker and Brook put down Renshaw in his 55 and Tom Banton put down a sitter late on – will frustrate, given Brook and the management have spoken of a wish of becoming the best fielding side in the world.

But, after poor run in ODIs which included a failed defence of the World Cup in 2023 and the dismal showing at last year's Champions Trophy, England's 50-over team ends in a much better place than it started.

By having Spencer Johnson caught, Brook even nipped in with the final wicket of the match - his first in ODIs.

Sports.title: The 3pm football blackout: Outdated or still relevant in 2026?
Sports.text:
After 60 years, is time finally running out on the 3pm blackout in football?

With pretty much every available television slot now exhausted, next year the Premier League and the EFL are set to hold serious discussions about its future.

There are concerns, especially within non-league football, that removing the blackout could have detrimental effects on attendances and finances.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham agrees, urging caution and suggesting the health of the football pyramid should come first.

But many Premier League fans feel they are short-changed, locked out of many of their team's fixtures just because they live in this country.

Go anywhere else in the world, and every single match is available live.

With streaming so prevalent, to some the blackout feels archaic.

Yet it is a complex situation, and many feel the depth of English football's pyramid is like nowhere else.

BBC Sport looks at the history of the blackout, why it is unique to British football and the arguments for and against keeping it.

It is the start of the 1964-65 season and the BBC launches a programme called Match of the Day.

Highlights of one match would be broadcast on BBC Two, a channel which at the time was only available in London.

Yet some clubs were concerned. Would fans still turn up to games?

Burnley chairman Bob Lord was the first owner to refuse to allow the cameras into Turf Moor. At the end of the season, several other clubs tried to block the renewal of the deal.

A compromise was reached and the BBC agreed not to reveal the televised Saturday match until all games had ended.

Shortly afterwards came the blackout for live matches.

Fast forward 20 years to 1987. With dwindling attendances across the European domestic leagues, partly influenced by crowd trouble, Uefa took up England's idea.

Article 48 was added to the Uefa Statutes.

Each country could designate a two-and-a-half-hour "transmission-free period", as long as at least 50% of matches in the top two leagues were taking place.

This was "designed to ensure that spectators are not deterred from attending local football matches of any kind and/or participating in matches at amateur and/or youth level".

Today, the situation has gone full circle. The only leagues that apply Article 48 are England, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

The reason for this is simpler than you might imagine.

No other major country qualifies for the blackout - because no other major country has a kick-off time that runs from the top flight and through the divisions.

It is a tradition that is unique to football in the United Kingdom.

Let's take Germany, often held up as an example of a country with excellent attendances despite not having a blackout.

This misses a key point. The Bundesliga has its own kick-off slot, 3:30pm on a Saturday, and no other division plays at the same time. The 2. Bundesliga, for instance, has a standard Saturday kick-off time of 1:30pm.

Could you imagine English football replicating this?

The other top leagues are the same.

In Spain, it is rare for either of the top two divisions to have games that kick off simultaneously. Each match has its own slot, and is broadcast live.

In Italy, Serie A plays on a Sunday afternoon, and Serie B on a Saturday.

In France, Ligue 1 has Saturday night as its main time slot, Ligue 2 plays largely on a Friday night, and Ligue 3 on a Saturday lunchtime.

So there is no blackout, because the football calendar works in a completely different way.

The next television rights cycle presents a unique opportunity.

The deals for the Premier League, EFL and Scottish Premiership are all up for renewal in 2029-30.

There is the chance for all the top stakeholders to come together and agree to end the blackout.

Last year, Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said there were no plans to remove the blackout.

But this summer there was a clear shift in emphasis, with Masters admitting there would be talks with the EFL ahead of the renewal of TV rights.

Scottish football has gone first, with broadcasters invited to bid to show all matches live - and is open to those shown on a Saturday afternoon.

It will be another year before we discover what the Premier League and the EFL - which seriously considered ending the blackout three years ago - are prepared to offer to broadcasters.

So, why would the leagues need to offer up the Saturday 3pm slot to broadcasters? After all, the latest domestic Premier League deal was worth a record £6.7bn - an increase of 4%.

However, to achieve that figure, the Premier League had to make an additional 70 games available. In real terms, it means each live Premier League game is worth less than it was before.

Now every single game not shown at 3pm on a Saturday - and there are only 110 left - is on TV.

Could the Premier League need to offer more matches for the rights to keep their overall value?

If so there are two options: try to find more TV slots, or show games at 3pm on a Saturday.

Could the Women's Super League benefit too? It looked into playing a 3pm on a Saturday but could not find a way around the blackout.

Most of the competition's games are shown live already, with a greater concern being stadium availability and consistency of kick-off times.

There is a danger that the issue of the 3pm blackout is viewed only through the lens of Premier League and EFL television rights.

But it goes much deeper than that.

Tom Greatrex, the chair of the Football Supporters' Association, says there are attendances in non-league football that some top flights in Europe "would look at jealously".

"We have one of the strongest football pyramids in the world, with excellent matchday attendances deep into the non-league game," Greatrex said.

"The prime minister is right to point out the value of the blackout to clubs further down the pyramid, and to urge caution over the impact rushed change could have on the overall health of the game."

BBC Sport understands that senior executives at the National League, which has a long-term global streaming deal with DAZN, are steadfastly against the blackout ending.

It has serious reservations, shared by the vast majority of its 72 clubs, that attendances would be impacted.

Included in this is transient attendance from season ticket holders of league clubs, many of whom go to non-league football when their team is away from home, boosting receipts considerably.

The fear is this could be lost if all league games are streamed at 3pm.

Nick Boom, the chair of Northern Premier League side FC United of Manchester, worries that the issue is only viewed through the lens of top-flight football.

"Football doesn't begin and end with the Premier League," Boom told BBC Sport.

"Every Saturday, thousands of people turn out to support their local clubs.

"For many of those clubs, the income from people coming through the turnstiles, buying a pint or something to eat is what keeps them alive.

"The 3pm blackout isn't about nostalgia. It's about protecting something that matters."

Boom added that clubs in non-league football are huge community assets, and losing them would have an impact "well beyond 90 minutes on a Saturday".

Some clubs are more open-minded about what ending the blackout could mean for non-league football.

Others have changed the way they operate to get around it.

North West Counties League Premier Division side FC Isle of Man have stopped playing at 3:00pm on a Saturday so they can stream all their games live.

Brian Shotton, a director at eighth-tier Ashington FC, told BBC Sport that he would not be automatically against removing the blackout.

"I would still have concerns, because every person through the gate makes a difference," Shotton said.

"I don't think we should just assume it would damage non-league football, but equally you need to know what it could mean for clubs like ours."

Ashington, who have attendances of about 400, see gates rise by up to 25% when Newcastle are not at home - but they already feel the impact of illegal streaming of the Magpies' games.

For the official broadcasters like Sky Sports, these supporters are seen as lost revenue.

There is an argument that the blackout drives piracy. Just how many of those particular fans would pay for a legal subscription is open to debate.

Added to that, there are now many weekends when fewer than 50% of matches in the top two divisions are played at 3pm on a Saturday anyway.

For instance, on 28 November there are just two in the Premier League, and seven in the Championship.

Other non-league clubs, like Dorking Wanders and Hashtag United, have spoken of the opportunities ending the blackout could bring, such as more income streams and fewer inconvenient kick-off times.

But this, for now, seems to be a minority view. The concerns for the health of the entire pyramid, on attendances and finances, are real.

Once the blackout is gone, it is unlikely to come back.

Sports.title: Alexander Zverev to defend himself against fresh lawsuit from ex-partner Brenda Patea
Sports.text:
Lawyers for world number one Alexander Zverev say he will defend himself against a lawsuit which alleges he misrepresented the outcome of his domestic abuse trial.

Former partner Brenda Patea is seeking damages and an injunction against him making similar comments in future.

In October 2023 Zverev was issued with a penalty order for bodily harm against Patea, with whom he has a daughter.

He contested the order, having always denied the charges, and a public trial was under way in Berlin in June 2024 when the court terminated the proceedings.

"The decision is not a verdict and it is not a decision about guilt or innocence," the court told the BBC.

"One decisive factor for the decision was that the witness has expressed her wish to end the trial. The defendant agreed to the termination of the case."

The court said there had been a separate settlement between Zverev and Patea.

But in September - as first reported by the Bounces website - lawyers for Patea filed a civil complaint in Berlin about an interview Zverev gave to French newspaper L'Equipe in June the day after he won his first Grand Slam title at Roland Garros.

According to the complaint, L'Equipe reported that Zverev allegedly said "my innocence has been proven".

The lawsuit asks that Zverev should be ordered "on pain of a fine of up to 250,000 euros (£209,000)" not to repeat the claim, and also seeks damages for the impact these statements have made on Patea.

"He was not found guilty, but he was not acquitted and they signed an agreement in which he committed not to talk about this case any more," Patea's lawyer Michael Scheele told BBC Sport.

"Instead he has said that it has been proven that he was not guilty. It's simply false.

"She doesn't want this to be repeated, because she's a content creator, an influencer, and she was accused of trying to make money, which was not true. If that had been the case, she would have asked in that [original] agreement to be compensated.

"He made a payment for the daughter, but nothing for her. She did not get any money."

Zverev is being represented by Berlin law firm Schertz Bergmann, which said: "Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit.

"If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion protected by Article 5(1) of the German Basic Law.

"Our client would merely have expressed his personal conviction that he had done everything in his power to refute the allegations made against him and that he considers his innocence to have been confirmed by the outcome of the criminal proceedings.

"He is fully entitled to hold and express this view.

"The criminal proceedings were discontinued without any finding of guilt, and the presumption of innocence remains unaffected."

The out-of-court settlement in Berlin in June 2024 came on the day Zverev reached the French Open final for the first time.

In the subsequent news conference, he was asked by BBC Sport whether he had any reservations about missing the opportunity to clear his name entirely.

"That's what dropping the case is. That is innocence," Zverev replied.

"They're not going to drop the case if you're guilty. I don't know what translations you have, but that's what it means.

"Done. We move on. I never ever want to hear another question about the subject again. That goes out to everybody."

Sports.title: Josh Kerr: The Making of the Man Behind the Shades
Sports.text:
You know Josh Kerr, right?

The guy with the shades. The fastest man to ever run a mile. Scottish, but with a curious transatlantic accent. Slicked-back hair. Beard. Usually got a medal of some kind slung around his neck. No stranger to telling you what he thinks.

That's Kerr the competitor, one of the foremost faces in world athletics, and a man who rampaged around London's Olympic Stadium in three minutes 42.66 seconds in July to set a new world record - then followed it up with a home Commonwealth gold and an imperious triumph at the Ultimate Championship.

Kerr recognises the description, smiling as it's articulated. But is there another version of him? Speaking to him during one of his regular returns to Scotland from his New Mexico base, it becomes clear there is.

There's scant chat about records, medals and his enjoyably niggly rivalry with Jakob Ingebrigtsen.

Instead, he talks about disguising alcohol-free cider, entering races under a false name, cold-calling universities, being starstruck meeting Scotland's rugby players and his granny keeping him humble.

This is the Kerr who spent the thick end of an hour on a chilly August evening taking selfies, signing his name and sharing his wisdom with young fans at Scotstoun after his Commonwealth medal presentation.

The Kerr who is still a regular visitor to first club Edinburgh AC's training sessions. This is Uncle Josh, who is heading for a party with his nephews after this chat.

The difference between the two versions of Kerr? The shades.

"They really help me switch my personality into work mode," he tells BBC Sport. "I think everyone has a work persona and it's a bit more intensified when it comes to my sport.

"Not a lot of things matter when I'm focused on my job, but the rest of the 23 hours and 56-and-a-bit minutes of the day, it's very different."

Kerr is sitting in the bay window of his parents' dining room as the autumnal gloom gathers in this desirable part of Edinburgh. All grand facades, imposing trees and permit parking.

His granny lives at the end of the road. His brother Jake and his family are 20 minutes outside the city. His school – the prestigious George Watson's – is a mile away.

The house has been home since Josh was five months old. Even now, this is where he returns on his five or six trips back to Scotland each year from his Albuquerque base, albeit the "chaos" of his teenage bedroom has long since been vanquished.

"It brings all different sorts of emotions," Kerr says of walking back through the terraced property's teal front door at the start of each visit. "As a kid, I would train from here every day. Everything started from that door.

"It's nice to fall back into that routine when I'm here. I can see the splits I'm running in my loops versus when I was 15. Slightly quicker..."

Around him in the room, pictures of the two brothers fight for space with memorabilia from their careers and assorted artwork. Jake - like their father John - was a professional rugby player, earning a cap for Scotland in the 2019 Six Nations.

He is 18 months older so served as not just an example to follow, but also a target to catch when Josh started racing at the age of nine, having caught the eye at a summer camp.

"If anyone ever wants to nerd out on the family stats, Jake has a pretty awesome under-15 cross-country record," Kerr says.

"We raced a couple of times, once at the Scottish cross-country relays when I ran under someone else's name because they didn't turn up, which was very hush-hush. I just followed him around, holding on for dear life.

"He still likes to remind me that I've never had an unbeaten season and he has. He still thinks he can beat me. That's the solid Kerr delusion in him. But it got me this far, so I can't question it."

The 29-year-old hasn't always had that familial brashness, though.

Dad John says "you wouldn't believe how quiet he was" as a child, speculating that Jake did his talking for him. And mum Jill, who has a background in tennis and is now her son's lead physio, recalls his "kindness and emotional intelligence".

Like all good parents, they are also a source of more esoteric anecdotes. Jill remembers providing both boys breakfasts in bed on competition days and teasing Josh for his "showboating", while John reveals that the teenager turned up to parties with non-alcoholic booze or arrived home sweating if he did have a beer, having run all the way back.

"Those are pretty niche stories," Kerr says, perhaps making a mental note to clamp his father later. "Everyone was starting to get into beers and things like that but it was just not really my thing. I found you could just rip the non-alcoholic bit off the label and get on with the socialising."

By that stage, any ambitions of following his dad and brother into rugby - as a full-back in his case - had been shelved, and his attention focused on athletics.

Kerr "wasn't a phenom by any means" and recalls winning races only "now and again", but the quiet kid had developed a resolve that running would be his future.

"Someone's got to be the best in the world, so why not me? That's what I had in my head," he explains. "I wanted to be a pro athlete and I knew running was going to be my ticket to that. The next stage for me was to go to university and get that paid for."

The problem was his athletic record, while good, wasn't stellar. And neither were his academic grades. Kerr needed to hustle.

He enlisted the help of his parents and fellow Edinburgh AC luminary Chris O'Hare to compile a list of US colleges and compose a CV and cover letter, then set about selling himself.

"I was 16 and just whipping emails out left, right and centre, saying: 'Hey, I'm coming over in 2015, do you have a spot for me?' And it was a pretty big no across the board," says Kerr, who re-read all the rejection emails recently.

"Then New Mexico said 'we'll take you' and I was like, 'perfect, I'll be there'. I told my parents and their first question was 'are they going to pay your fees?' and I was like 'uhm, well, I didn't ask'. So they made me phone back and check!"

He did and they were, which set in motion the move that would change Kerr's life in more ways than one.

It was on his first week in Albuquerque, while on a campus bus that his parents blagged their way on to posing as professors, that Kerr met Larimar Rodriguez, who became his wife last year.

"It was a big week," he says. "It's one of those ones where you don't really realise until you look back.

"I met Larimar when I was 17 and I'm incredibly proud of her. She's done four years of undergrad, four years of med school, and now she's in her fourth year of residency. She'll be a full attending dermatologist by June or July."

Josh and Larimar live together in New Mexico with their mini schnauzer El Presidente, who often joins Kerr on his lighter runs.

That's part of a precisely-honed routine that starts with alternate ice baths and hot tub dips at 5am, and some visualisation and journaling around breakfast before he "goes to work" at the track or in the gym from 10am-2pm.

The next three hours are spent in his bedroom, which has been adapted to serve as an altitude chamber, before he retires for the day before 9pm.

The attention to detail is startling. Childhood friend and fellow former world 1500m champion Jake Wightman recounts sharing a room with bronze medallist Kerr at the Tokyo Olympics and looking on in bemusement as he unpacked a scented diffuser, mattress topper and waffle maker to replicate being at home.

Five years on, Kerr has a team of 16 in his Brooks Beast running family under head coach Danny Mackey, including personal chef Jameel, a mental performance consultant and a chiropractor.

It's a long way from life behind that teal door in Edinburgh, but how different is Kerr now from the one who left his homeland 11 years ago? "Pretty similar," he says, while acknowledging that he is now more outwardly confident of his abilities.

That "abrasive, calling-your-shot side" as he calls it, is not a traditional trait for a Scot but has been shaped by more than a decade in the United States and by his desire to shine a light on athletics.

"Everyone says, 'oh, we're not getting attention' but go out and earn it," Kerr says. "Make people want to care about what you're doing.

"I'm an individual business and I'm trying as hard as I can to bring eyeballs because I think athletics is the purest form of sport. It didn't really come naturally to me before - being in the US has kind of shaped me a little bit - but I hope people realise that the reason I'm in this position is the blood that runs through my veins.

"I'm able to represent the UK a lot more than I'm able to represent Scotland, but it's such a huge part of who I am. And I hope they take great pride in the performances I'm able to produce.

"I've been inspired by some incredible athletes and I guess this is my turn to step up and try and bridge the gap between grassroots and where I'm at."

Kerr has done that on the track, with two Olympic medals to add to his world indoor and outdoor golds, but he is approaching a stage where his celebrity might breach the confines of athletics.

Take last week. On a four-day visit home, his duties as Uncle Josh were surrounded by a glut of sponsorship and media engagements - including an appearance on the BBC's flagship current affairs programme Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg - as well as a coaching session with young athletes and an invitation to carry out the match ball at Murrayfield before Scotland faced New Zealand.

Of course, the omnipresent spectre of BBC Sports Personality of the Year is looming into view, too. Kerr, it should be noted, is not shy in coveting that prize.

That he will likely be one of the main contenders speaks to how life has changed for him in the past couple of years.

Kerr can still enjoy being back in Edinburgh in relative peace - "I got recognised at the end of the street recently… it was my granny" - but concedes life in America can be a bit more challenging because of requests for "400 selfies and a video for their nan".

That attention will only intensify over the coming months should he complete the one or two outstanding items on his athletics tick list and frank his ambition of being "remembered as the best middle-distance athlete of all time".

While he is waiting to see how his winter training goes before 'calling his shot' again, Kerr has other world records in his sights and, of course, Los Angeles in 2028 and a chance to complete the full set of Olympic medals by winning gold.

Silver was not what he wanted in Paris, albeit the passing of time has allowed some satisfaction with the British record he ran, so righting that wrong in the States is top of his agenda.

Kerr has already made a low-key visit to the Colosseum, the epic venue two hours from his New Mexico home where the athletics events will be staged, to help visualise the moment - just as he did with the Stade de France.

He will be back again before the shades go on and he gets down to the business of proving himself to be the best ever.

Sports.title: Australia sandpapergate: Cameron Bancroft claims whole team knew of plot in South Africa
Sports.text:
Cameron Bancroft has claimed the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot in explosive revelations that will heap pressure on current captain Pat Cummins.

In a detailed testimony, published by the West Australian,, external batter Bancroft - the player caught with the sandpaper during the Test match against South Africa - has given arguably the most complete account of the events in Cape Town eight years ago.

"In 2018 not the entire truth was told," said Bancroft. "I have never been completely honest about what happened."

For the past two weeks, Australian cricket has been embroiled in a debate over the ball-tampering saga following the publication of Usman Khawaja's autobiography.

Khawaja wrote that the whole Australia team knew of the plot, claims supported by David Warner and Chadd Sayers. Cummins described Khawaja's account as "wrong" and "nonsense".

On the day Cricket Australia announced a forum into the sandpaper episode, Bancroft published his account, explaining he was motivated by the news conference given by Cummins.

"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference," said Bancroft.

"It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.

"What I saw, experienced and lived with - not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa - is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time."

Khawaja's autobiography and the subsequent claims made by Warner and seamer Sayers have reopened old wounds related to the sandpaper saga.

Still, those connected have remained true to the accounts they have presented during the intervening eight years.

The most significant denial came from Cummins, who rebuffed Khawaja's account in an extraordinary 68-minute address to the media in Sydney. Lehmann and Starc have also reiterated their denials.

Now, it is the extensive detail provided by Bancroft that could shed a whole new light on the controversy and lead to further questions for Cummins, Lehmann and Cricket Australia.

Cummins is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand on 9 December.

A statement released on behalf of Cummins said: "Whilst we feel for Cam and everything he's been through there's nothing in the statement that hasn't been answered by Pat in his press conference."

A Cricket Australia statement said: "We respect that Cameron Bancroft has told his story, and we will take time to consider his comments.

"We expect that there will be many dimensions to the events of 2018, which is why we have established the forum for individuals to give their version of events.

"We are finalising the terms of reference and will commence the process as soon as possible."

In his account, Bancroft said: "I have spent eight years speaking about accountability, honesty and the lessons I learned from one of Australian cricket's darkest moments.

"However, in 2018 not the entire truth was told. I have never been completely honest about what happened.

"It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team.

"When I was questioned during Cricket Australia's investigation, I did not give a complete and truthful account.

"I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others.

"I did this to protect Cricket Australia's investigation and not implicate others around me."

Bancroft said his actions were "discussed" and "acknowledged" by the entire playing group at the end of the second day and before the beginning of the third day. He said he was encouraged by Saker, who has since worked as a consultant with England.

The only person within the camp to express unease at the ball-tampering, according to Bancroft, was media manager Kate Hutchison.

"I received wraps and encouragement from members of the playing and coaching staff, especially David Saker," said Bancroft.

"Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening.

"I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion.

"I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up.

"Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it."

Bancroft identifies Saker as the coach Khawaja claimed encouraged him to work harder on the ball during the third Test in Cape Town. The 33-year-old said he took "feedback" from all the bowlers and wicketkeeper Tim Paine, who took over the captaincy when Smith was sacked.

In Cape Town, Bancroft was confronted by the umpires when TV cameras showed him concealing the sandpaper in his trousers. He claimed Lehmann sent a message to him via Handscomb.

"Peter Handscomb ran out at the drinks break after I'd been caught and shoved the sandpaper down my pants," wrote Bancroft.

"He said to me: 'I think it's time I take that off you now.' And Pete was doing his job after Boof [Lehmanm] shouted to him on the walkie talkie "get the sandpaper off Bangers [Bancroft] now".

"If he didn't know he wouldn't have said that. And if it wasn't clear enough before, then it was obvious now."

In 2021, Bancroft was playing county cricket with Durham and gave an interview to The Guardian in which he said the bowlers' involvement in the plot was "self-explantory".

In response, Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and spinner Nathan Lyon released a joint-statement denying any knowledge that ball-tampering had taken place.

"Reading that statement was deeply painful," said Bancroft.

"I had memories of conversations on the field in Port Elizabeth and Newlands, feedback about the ball and shared celebrations that made the statement difficult for me to digest."

For almost two weeks, Australian cricket has been at war with itself over the revelations in Usman Khawaja's autobiography.

But there has been an absence of a smoking gun. Without tangible, new, hard evidence, all that was left was claim and counter-claim.

Naturally, the spotlight fell on Pat Cummins because of his role as a bowler in Cape Town and his elevation to Australia captain in the years since.

His performance last week in front of the media, on live television, was extraordinary. For 68 minutes he took all questions and appeared plausible in his answers.

In being so robust in his denial of Khawaja's account - Cummins called it "nonsense" - the skipper also left himself open to the consequences if it was later revealed he was not telling the truth.

Crucially, it was Cummins' press conference that compelled Cameron Bancroft to speak out.

It must be stressed that Bancroft's account is not the open-and-shut evidence that convicts Cummins or anyone else in the dressing room at Newlands in 2018.

But it is certainly the most complete account we have heard from anyone involved, walking step-by-step through the genesis of the plot, the execution and the fallout. Bancroft has named names: Cummins, the other bowlers, Tim Paine, coach Darren Lehmann and assistant coach David Saker. It is, potentially, the decisive intervention that shifts this whole saga in a new direction.

Whether by accident or design, it came on the day Cricket Australia (CA) announced its forum for evidence into the sandpaper controversy. Before Bancroft's account CA's action felt an unsatisfactory halfway house - not an investigation, with no guarantee outcomes will be published.

What now? Will CA go further? How will those implicated by Bancroft respond? How can Cummins lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand? Could Steve Smith break a silence he has held since the publication of Khawaja's book?

Throughout the past fortnight, there has been a sense that Australian cricket hoped the sandpaper debate would eventually go away. Cummins even said he never wanted to speak about it again.

Instead of fading, the thirst for the truth grows, now fuelled by Bancroft's extraordinary story.
