articles.title: Formula 1 in Las Vegas, Miami and Austin - how do the races compare?
articles.text:
"The picnic blanket that you'd happily sit on in Austin will get confiscated by security at Miami and will end up wrapped around you in the chill of a Vegas night."

Cadence Kim from Dallas lives the reality of being an avid Formula 1 fan in the United States, in the three diverse locations the sport now frequents. She will be among the 300,000 spectators around the iconic Las Vegas Strip this weekend.

Las Vegas joined the F1 calendar in 2023, a year after Miami, while Austin has been home to the United States Grand Prix since 2012.

Kim has put in the hard yards travelling across the Atlantic to witness F1 in its European heartland. Now she is reaping the rewards of owners Liberty Media investing heavily in the three US races, which have all recently been awarded new long-term contracts.

"Following F1 from the US used to mean accepting a massive barrier to entry," Kim explains.

"It meant setting an early alarm and trying to explain to room mates why you were yelling at 20 rich men driving funny-looking cars very quickly. It was more of a niche sport with no natural gathering places for a community to watch. What bar is open at that time?

"Having three domestic races has changed everything. It has shifted F1 from a purely broadcast experience into something tangible. It becomes a week-long experience where a fan gets to engage with a like-minded community, attend parties in the evening, and do a meet-and-greet. You can walk a track, sit in a grandstand, purchase the overpriced merch, hear the engines and literally feel a part of something."

The community Kim is attached to is the ATX GP Club, formed in Austin by Maria Rodriguez and Julia Wezio, where watch parties help fans learn more about the sport and the drivers. With the longest running of the US races on their doorstep, at the Circuit of the Americas, she's ideally placed to compare all three venues for the fan experience.

"Vegas is a party," exclaims Kim. "The Nevada desert gets cold at night, so the cowboy hat doesn't make the trip, but socks, a hoodie and gloves do.

"Many of the teams have hotel partnerships so lobbies become team activation zones, and you might end up sharing an elevator with an engineer. The fan flow is well managed with everyone being funnelled through specific pedestrian walkways, but if you do have a ticket to watch the race at the track you are limited to staying only in that one specific zone.

"Vegas is known for its dining but that doesn't make it to the track. Ticketing forces you to consider some pretty rigid trade-offs. For example, sitting at Turn One means missing the musical artists and activations by the Sphere.

"As for Austin, you aren't restricted to a single assigned area but can walk almost the entire perimeter of the track. With each of the three races you get a local vibe integrated into the entertainment. It's not an artificially manufactured aesthetic in Austin, you're getting real Texas BBQ, smoked brisket and bedazzled cowboy hats.

"I've been once to Miami and would not consider going back unless it became a night race. The South Florida sun bakes both the track and the attendees during the daytime. Preparing for an outdoor trek is the best mindset. Treat it like a multi-day hike where you'll be logging 30,000 steps each day so comfortable shoes and water with electrolyte packets are a must."

The excitement level of racing at the Las Vegas Grand Prix in its opening three years has been as bright as the neon lights on the Strip. The debut race in 2023 was an instant classic, with the lead changing hands five times, and drama all the way to the line as Charles Leclerc overtook Sergio Perez for second place, behind winner Max Verstappen.

It was instant payback for F1, who had invested more than £500m in buying land and promoting the event. Despite complaints from some local residents and businesses over the disruption to the city streets, the gamble has paid dividends, according to Vegas-based podcast host and nine-time Le Mans 24 Hours driver Justin Bell.

"I was telling people, 'just wait'. It's like a big piece of Ikea furniture – once you do it once, it's so much quicker and more efficient the next time," Bell tells BBC Sport.

"The promoters did listen to the locals and worked out ways to get them involved, by offering discounted tickets and attempting to minimise the disruption. Let's face it, Las Vegas exists for one reason and that is to entertain visitors, and with the extraordinary economic impact it has I am sure the pros outweigh the cons for almost everyone involved."

That economic impact has been valued at $3.2bn for the Southern Nevada region over the three years, with each of the 175,000 visitors from outside Las Vegas spending an average of $2,400 on non-racing activities, according to figures from the 2024 race.

Bell, who presents the Drive to Wynn podcast from the luxury resort on the Strip, and used to guide celebrities like Drew Barrymore and Steve Carell in race cars on the Jay Leno Show, thinks Vegas has the perfect opportunity to position itself as the premier US race, despite it being the youngest.

"Vegas has such a leg up on the other two locations as a global entertainment hub, that aligns so well with the direction that F1 is heading as a brand," he says. "Miami is sexy and in theory has much going for it, but the track itself isn't in Miami so there are the usual inconveniences in terms of transportation.

"In contrast, I always recommended Austin to F1 newcomers as a track to visit first, because it is a purpose-built facility that is so easy to spectate at, with tons of room to walk around and watch cars from every angle all while eating a hotdog.

"From the first laps from 2023, it became evident that the Vegas track design was going to be great for F1. The mix of tight corners with that long straight down the iconic Strip invites breathtaking overtaking. Each successive year gets better."

One of the burning questions, as to whether F1 can sustain its upward growth curve of popularity in the United States, is whether an American driver needs to be part of the elite 24 on the grid.

Logan Sargeant was the last American to drive in an F1 grand prix, in the Netherlands in August 2024. Contenders for future seats include Cadillac reserve driver Colton Herta, Jak Crawford and Ugo Ugochukwu, the 2026 Formula 3 champion.

"Thanks to Drive to Survive, this new breed of American F1 fan is attracted to the global superstar drivers," says Bell.

"They are exciting, handsome and wealthy. If the right American driver does make it to F1 he has to be a rock star both on and off the track. Colton might be fast enough but is he a media darling? I am not convinced that unless whomever he is ticks all those boxes, that it will really make a difference to the US fanbase. Americans like winners, not just participants."

Kim agrees that F1 is inherently global: "It doesn't bother me at all. I am a fan of an Australian and a Dutch driver while being an American with a Polish background. When I moved from Austin to Dallas this past summer, I wasn't handed a welcome kit by the Dallas Cowboys and told that now they expect my support.

"US representation already exists with Haas and Cadillac, but I don't think that we need an American driver on the grid for Americans to tune in and show up."

Crawford, Aston Martin's reserve driver, is one of those aiming to be that next American F1 star. Speaking to BBC Sport, he sees a growing percentage of younger drivers already leaning towards F1 ahead of the traditional Nascar and IndyCar series.

"I have a lot of kids and kart drivers coming up to me, and say that I inspire them, and I'm not on the grid full time. So I can't even imagine what that would be like if I was," Crawford says.

"I went to the first Austin race, in 2012, as a seven-year old. Back then it was hard to find how to watch F1 in the United States. Over time, as I raced in Europe, I became more passionate about it, and I grew up hand in hand with the popularity of F1 in the US.

"Austin is a phenomenal circuit. I'm biased as I'm from Texas. Las Vegas is cool, as a night race. I raced a lot there in karting, on a street circuit, and it's very cool driving past the big casinos at night."

Las Vegas is the Marmite of the three US races for me. You either love it or hate it, and somehow I manage to feel both ways about it over the course of the same weekend.

I've always struggled slightly with Vegas as a destination. Unless you're there for a very particular sort of weekend, I think the novelty can wear off surprisingly quickly. It's an extraordinary place to look at, but outside the circuit and paddock, the sensory overload can become exhausting. There are only so many flashing lights, casinos and enormous hotels you can take before you start craving somewhere a little more normal.

The timings don't help either. Everything happens so late, and the desert temperatures can be surprisingly cold once the sun goes down. Combined with the expense of the weekend, it isn't necessarily the easiest or most relaxing grand prix to attend.

However, one huge advantage of Vegas is that you barely need to get in a car once you've arrived. Apart from the journey between the airport and your hotel, so much of the grand prix experience is within walking distance. Compared with the traffic in Miami, that's a real luxury.

And of course, the moment you see Formula 1 cars racing down the Las Vegas Strip at night, an awful lot of those complaints disappear.

It is genuinely one of the most spectacular sights in motorsport. We've become so accustomed to seeing Formula 1 cars at purpose-built circuits or traditional street tracks, but watching them fly past some of the most recognisable landmarks in the world, illuminated by the lights of Vegas, is pretty extraordinary.

They really know how to put on a show, too. The entertainment doesn't simply stop when the chequered flag falls. The post-race spectacle is another part of the experience, and it's difficult to think of another grand prix that embraces that side of Formula 1 quite so enthusiastically.

For all my reservations about Vegas as a destination, I completely understand why someone would want to experience the race at least once. There really is nothing else like it.

Overall, Austin is where I'd send someone who loves the racing, Miami is where I'd send someone who wants the best all-round grand prix holiday and Las Vegas is where I'd send someone who wants to experience something they won't forget.

For me, Miami wins, although there's something about Austin that still feels like the soul of American Formula 1. And despite all my complaints about Vegas, there's absolutely no denying the spectacle of seeing those cars flying down the Strip at night.

articles.title: Carla Ward: Republic of Ireland manager close to agreeing contract extension
articles.text:
Republic of Ireland manager Carla Ward says she is close to agreeing a contract extension, as she named her squad for their 2027 Women's World Cup play-off final with Poland.

The former Aston Villa manager replaced Eileen Gleeson at the helm in January 2025 and has led the side to promotion to League A in the Nations League and their highest ever position in the Uefa rankings.

The Republic of Ireland have lost just one of their past six games and now face Poland in a play-off for a spot at the World Cup in Brazil next summer.

Ward's side travel to Gdansk for the first leg on 1 December before the reverse fixture four days later at Dublin's Aviva Stadium.

The 42-year-old's current deal expires at the end of the 2027 World Cup qualification cycle.

Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said earlier this month that there were "live conversations" around Ward's contract.

"I want to get one thing straight - last time I said I wanted to focus on the next four games," said Ward.

"What I mean by that is, I want the focus to be on the players and certainly not myself.

"But what I can say to everybody is, I think you all know that I love being here. I want to be here. I have absolutely no intention of going anywhere.

"Thankfully, the FAI feel the same. So yes, just to echo David's words, we're close. And look, we're happy. I'm happy. So, yeah, I'm sure you'll have me for a little bit longer."

articles.title: Anthropic: The seven founders about to become multi-billionaires
articles.text:
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.

The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.

Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each.

If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each.

So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?

In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.

He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.

Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.

Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.

But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.

Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".

Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.

She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.

Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.

She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.

The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.

Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.

He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.

Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.

He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".

Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.

Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.

Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.

He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.

Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.

Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.

McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.

He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

articles.title: Nvidia reports bumper results as firm says it's not reinstating Jensen Huang
articles.text:
Nvidia has firmly ruled out letting ousted co-founder Jensen Huang return as it revealed that sales doubled to more than $100bn.

In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit last week, covering the three month period just before the recent scandal surfaced, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it was "business as usual". She told investors: "We've got this."

Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.

But Nvidia's chair Harvey Jones said: "The board does not intend to reinstate him."

Nvidia reported that sales for the three months to 25 October rose to $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading.

The company's profits also doubled from a year ago rising to $65bn. Sales from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn.

The company said its rapid growth is poised to continue and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.

Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.

"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."

Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry.

"It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."

She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects".

"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."

The interim chief executive also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.

The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.

They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.

Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.

Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.

He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection.

"With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new chief executive will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."

Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia.

The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media.

Nvidia's strong earnings are "from the machine that Jensen built" and a company tends to lose "its shine and vision" after an iconic founder leaves, Monaghan said.

articles.title: How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
articles.text:
Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.

That partnership has now ended following Huang's resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which is alleged to have been with a Chinese spy.

The company has been rocked by the scandal, with hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value and questions swirling about the extent of the impact of Huang's departure.

While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.

The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.

Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.

It is now one the most valuable firms, worth $3.8 trillion (£2.9 trillion), and on Tuesday said its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.

But there's now an air of uncertainty over Nvidia's future direction. Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on the company, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at investment firm AJ Bell, says because Huang was also a key figure in "flying the flag" to drum up enthusiasm and investment for the wider AI industry, his departure posed a "real risk" that Nvidia could now decide to change its current strategy and rein in spending.

Such a move could spell a wider slowdown in AI investment, which would have an economic impact. How big? That's "unknown", Coatsworth says.

"If they decide to go with the much more cautious route... there could be a knock-on effect in that you have got various companies in the AI infrastructure space suddenly finding they don't have a key source of finance," he says.

Kunjan Sobhani, senior technology industry analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, expects the impact of Huang leaving to be "limited" for now as Nvidia has strong commitments and a deep order book. But he said this picture could change in the long run.

That is because Nvidia, on its journey to the top of the AI industry, has created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".

Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.

The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?

That risk is perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, have called for Huang's reinstatement.

Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, which has also prompted a campaign by shareholders and supporters to "Bring Jensen Back".

Huang himself has said he is open to a return, just days after resigning.

Coatsworth says he has never seen circular financing used at this scale before, but admits there are competitive rivals around, which could insulate the wider AI industry from any potential slowdown at the firm.

When Nvidia's share price plunged in the wake of the affair revelations, the stock of its rival semiconductor makers including AMD, Broadcom and Marvell Technology jumped.

"I don't think all AI activity grinds to a halt if Nvidia slows down what it's doing and if it pulls some financing, but it does change how people would look at the whole situation," Coatsworth adds.

articles.title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave
articles.text:
"Photonic chips are on the verge of a breakthrough," says Ton van Mol of the Dutch research institute TNO.

If van Mol is right – and TNO, the European Union and the Dutch government are backing the idea with millions of euros - then the technology could be a gamechanger.

The chips which run today's society, from your phone and TV, to the vast data centres meeting our insatiable desire for AI, are mostly electrical.

They process data by shunting electrons around tiny circuits – a single microchip produced today can contain billions of transistors, and sizes are measured in nanometres (one nanometre is a billionth of a metre).

Because they use light instead of electricity, photonic chips are faster, use less energy and generate less heat than traditional computer chips.

Van Mol hopes for an acceleration in photonics similar to the one seen in electrical chips since the 1970s.

"With optical chips, you are now where electronic chips were maybe 40 [or] 50 years ago."

American, Taiwanese and Chinese firms dominate the computer chip industry, but Europe sees the emergence of photonic chips as a fresh opportunity to lead, on what could be, a key future technology.

Which is why the European Union has committed €400m ($450m; £330m) to a project called PIX Europe, external, with the stated goal of making the continent "a global leader in emerging technology for Photonic Integrated Chips".

"Europe said 'we need to have our own manufacturing in-house'," says van Mol, who is leading a key part of the programme.

"We cannot depend like in the past that everything is manufactured in the US or China - that's not wise, so the [European] Chips Act was called into life, and one of the parts of the act is to build pilot lines to really bring the technology, which is now in labs, to the next stage - manufacturing."

Electronic and photonic chips are produced on wafers made up of hundreds of individual chips. Factories with machines that can handle bigger wafers can churn out chips more efficiently.

"[Photonic chip] manufacturing worldwide is [currently] done on wafers which are four inches (10cm) in size, and the next step is to scale-up production to a six-inch wafer," says van Mol.

His team are already building a 10,000 sq m factory to produce six-inch indium phosphide wafers on the High Tech Campus in the Dutch city of Eindhoven.

It's due to fully open in 2030 and will be a major step forward, not just for photonics in Europe, but around the world, according to van Mol.

"That's the development TNO is going to do, in a pilot line which is really serious.

"In 2030, we hope that we have a stable, reproducible, high-yield process, and then the intention is that the pilot line [opens] to industrial parties who can make commercial production out of it."

Europe does have one crucial player in the current computer chip industry - ASML.

The Netherlands-based tech giant is the only company in the world able to build the machines needed to make the most sophisticated semiconductors.

Which is why ASML products will sit at the heart of the pilot line in Eindhoven - it's no coincidence that van Mol's project is based around the corner from ASML's headquarters.

"The way you produce these [photonic] chips is very similar to the way you produce electrical or electronic chip," says van Mol.

"You use the same type of equipment, you also need a high-end clean room, you also use wafers, so the production method is very similar to the traditional semiconductor technology."

ASML itself is keen to explore the opportunities that the emerging technology of photonics could offer.

"Europe has a strong position in photonics research. The next challenge is translating those innovations into industrial-scale manufacturing," says Stanislas Baron, who is the head of ASML's EU/US Customer Team.

ASML's unique success has helped build an influential and lucrative network of companies and institutions devoted to semiconductor technology in and around Eindhoven, and it's a model for what Europe is trying to achieve with photonic chips.

The Eindhoven project has the backing of former ASML chief executive Peter Wennink, author of an influential report for the Dutch government called The Roadmap to Future Prosperity, external, which noted that the market for photonics was expected to grow 10 to 20 times in the next 10 years.

In a news release backing the new pilot line, Wennink described it as "a launchpad for Europe's future digital economy".

"By investing in scalable production capacity, we are creating an ecosystem that can help shape the global technological direction," he said.

Of course, Europe is not alone in looking to the potential of photonics to earn a global economic advantage.

In June this year, US photonics company Coherent announced what it called "the world's first and largest volume-production six-inch indium phosphide manufacturing platform" at its plant in Sherman, in Texas.

The expansion is backed by chip manufacturing giant Nvidia, external, as well as $50 million public funds under the US Chips Act.

It's an illustration of how quickly the market is moving, and how central photonic chips could be to the continuing race to retain an influential stake in AI and technological development more generally.

Europe's bid to establish itself as a global leader in photonic chips – exemplified by the Eindhoven project – is the kind of strategy that makes sense in a globalised economy, says Joris Teer, policy analyst at the European Institute for Security Studies in Brussels.

If the continent can take a lead in photonic chips, then future developments in AI and data will partly be dependent on Europe.

"Europe knows that its high energy and labour costs, skilled workforce shortages, and lack of private and public capital make an across-the-board reindustrialisation strategy impossible", Teer says.

"To retain influence, ensuring dependence on European parties rather than European autonomy is key."

Once up and running, the Eindhoven project will provide a pilot production line which can be used multiple companies.

It will be open to businesses across Europe and beyond, who can design and build chips without having to develop their own expensive production facilities.

"What we want to establish here is what we call a foundry model; there's no intention to have our own product," Ton van Mol says.

Instead, they will produce to order for outside customers.

It's the same idea which, at huge scale, has brought Taiwanese-based giant TSMC a position of global dominance in the manufacture of microchips.

Photonic chips are already in use, in highly specialised areas in data centres and in Lidar (light detection and ranging) sensor technology, for instance.

For van Mol of TNO, helping the industry to scale up, by easing production challenges and increasing capacity, is the key step to moving them into the tech we use in our daily lives, like phones and laptops, and to drive innovation in areas like medical scanners and 6G communications.

"The demand is there", says van Mol, "and the end goal is to have, in Europe, manufacturing of these chips, which is strategically very important because these chips [could] become the backbone of all data and telecom."

articles.title: Critical flaw found in vital internet language Java through AI
articles.text:
A cyber-security firm has used artificial intelligence (AI) to uncover a critical flaw in the hugely popular computer programming language Java.

Tech start-up Calif - which recently identified a cyber-security flaw in another language, PHP - found the bug in Java's memory functions.

Java is a popular programming language used by nearly all of the world's top companies such as Apple and Amazon, as well as many banks, hospitals and governments.

It is meant to make the IT world more secure by managing your memory online, said computer scientist Professor Toby Walsh, which is why "this is such an unlikely and serious flaw".

The discovery comes after a string of serious technology issues, including a massive Microsoft outage.

On Tuesday, the US National Security Agency said its internal communications went offline on Tuesday due to a "scheduled routine maintenance".

The NSA did not specify whether its outage was linked to the identified Java bug.

Apple also reported multiple services suffered full outages due to an internal update, while a network failure grounded all flights in the US.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the incidents were related.

With the help of AI, Calif discovered a serious security vulnerability it has called Java4Shell, which allowed an adversary to remotely execute unwanted commands to Java's memory system.

In this case, the adversary was OpenAI's recently-released model GPT-6 Cyber, which is not yet available to the public.

Oracle, the owner of Java, released a "critical patch update" on Tuesday, which it said contained security vulnerability fixes - including for this flaw.

At this stage it is unclear if any platforms or companies have been affected by the latest incident.

But the Java flaw remains a huge concern for cyber-security experts, who say overloading a system's memory is one of the most common ways for hackers to exploit or crash a system.

The BBC has contacted Oracle for comment.

Nearly every critical sector, including banking, national security systems, aviation and telecommunications, relies on Java.

First released in 1995, the programming language and computing system is now the "beating heart of the modern economy", Calif said in its investigation.

One of its main functions is to manage and protect memory for you, Walsh, a leading researcher in AI, told the BBC.

Any time you transfer information on the internet, receive a file from a user or need to log into an IT system with a password, the platform you are using is likely relying on a Java program.

The serious flaw could comprise "critical financial systems, customers and organisation's data," cyber-security expert Dr Pedram Hayati said.

In Australia alone, almost every bank uses Java for managing critical transaction data, Hayati added.

The latest incidents have exposed how nearly every critical sector - including national security systems, aviation and telecommunications - relies on legacy infrastructure online.

Earlier this week, thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, reported trouble accessing services.

The Java discovery follows a critical cyber-security flaw identified in the PHP programming language, also identified by Calif.

PHP is the code that websites like Wikipedia use to collect information and present it in a way you can read on the web.

Surrey Centre for Cyber Security Prof Alan Woodward said the PHP flaw affected some 30 million websites, leaving them vulnerable to malicious attacks.

At the time, website owners were urged to check if their sites were affected and, if so, they were told to install updates to patch the issue or consider going offline.

The PHP flaws went undetected for at least a decade, which Walsh said is similar to what has happened with Java.

"It's been hiding in plain sight for 12 years", he said.

"AI is now exposing more flaws much more quickly," Walsh said including ones that may have been so obscure and difficult that humans could not have discovered them alone.

Earlier in November, OpenAI president Greg Brockman announced his company was pivoting 25% of its staff to focus on cyber-security demands.

articles.title: Nvidia: China fears Jensen Huang scandal could shut it out of US AI tech before Xi-Trump summit
articles.text:
Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.

For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.

Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.

US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.

The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.

For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.

Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.

Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.

Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger.

Democrats, who will control Congress come January, have made their position clear. Last Wednesday top Democrat Ted Lieu told Politico the Trump administration had been "1,000%" too deferential to Nvidia, putting national security at risk, while fellow Democrat Zoe Lofgren suggested Congress would now be more likely to restrict sales of AI chips to China.

The BBC has approached the White House for comment.

Beijing's foreign ministry had described the spy claims as a "smear against China".

"The US should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives to find pretexts for imposing technological blockades," spokesperson Mao Ning said last week.

The ministry also seemed keen to keep the meeting on track, saying the two countries had kept "close communication regarding interactions between the two heads of state".

For the last year, Trump and Xi have been seeking to stabilise relations after a damaging tariff war that almost brought trade between the two countries to a standstill.

The Trump administration's decision to permit sales of advanced Nvidia H200 chips to China in late 2025 was seen as evidence that both sides were searching for areas of co-operation, even while competition intensified.

It was a rare move given Washington had spent years trying to limit China's access to the most advanced chips.

Many in the US have long viewed these chips as a national security issue, arguing they could strengthen China's military and surveillance capabilities. Jensen Huang, who rejects that claim, advocated lifting bans on the export of high-performing chips to China. Beijing argues the restrictions are an attempt to contain its rise.

Now that opening may be under threat.

History has taught Beijing and Washington that spy scandals rarely remain confined to the intelligence world.

Analysts in China already see echoes of an incident in 2023 when a suspected surveillance balloon drifted through the skies over the US before an American fighter jet shot it down. Beijing insisted it was a civilian meteorological airship that had strayed off course.

But a planned trip by then US Secretary of State Antony Blinken was cancelled and communication between the two governments deteriorated sharply.

The incident showed how quickly a security dispute could overwhelm diplomatic efforts and push relations into a deep freeze.

"The mere passage of a balloon sent American public opinion and politicians into a state of high alert, as if a "Chinese threat" were looming directly overhead," said the state media outlet, the Global Times this week as it made a direct comparison with the Nvidia scandal.

"No-one on the US side has ever apologised or taken responsibility for the genuine damage this caused to US-China relations," it added.

The state-run outlet also questioned why the Nvidia story had emerged so soon after "the hard-won detente" between Beijing and Washington, following a meeting between the two countries' leaders in September.

"Is someone behind the scenes pushing an agenda and stirring up confrontation?" it asked.

The summit is also being carefully choreographed by Beijing to show off its technological prowess in Shenzhen - a deeply symbolic choice of city.

It's home to some of the country's biggest tech companies and has become a showcase for Beijing's ambitions in AI and advanced manufacturing.

Also, given Washington's tighter restrictions on advanced chips, Beijing has options for retaliation.

One of its most powerful tools is its dominance of key rare earth minerals. China processes much of the world's supply for materials that are used in everything from electric vehicles and smartphones to military equipment.

Analysts have long warned that technological restrictions can trigger a cycle of retaliation in which each side reaches for its strongest economic leverage.

That would shift the current trend of US-China relations from engagement back towards mutual suspicion.

articles.title: GTA 6 reviews say highly-anticipated game is a masterpiece
articles.text:
After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.

Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?

According to the first reviews, it's a resounding yes.

Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100, external - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.

Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.

Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype."

But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN, external branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".

Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building.

"The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote, external, but he added "there are also nits to pick".

For The New York Times, external one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors.

Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action.

But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.

The graphics of the game were hotly anticipated and so far have not disappointed critics, with The Guardian, external describing Leonida, the setting inspired by Miami, as "so lifelike that at times it beggars belief".

And the relationship between the lead characters, Jason and Lucia, has also stunned critics.

"They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote, adding: "I found it impossible not to care for them".

Writing for Forbes, external, Paul Tassi said: "I can't say I've ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share".

The Washington Post, external said GTA 6 "raises the bar at every level", while Bloomberg, external's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in his five star review.

"It's hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here," he wrote. "There's nothing else like it.

"While playing this game, I often found myself wondering how it even exists."

Rockstar hasn't revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (£760m).

The Game Awards - the most watched ceremony of its kind in the industry - gave players a teaser of the critical reception when its 2026 nominations were revealed on Tuesday.

And despite having not released at the time, GTA 6 was the most-nominated title.

It will be up for eight prizes, including game of the year and best music.

The nomination of Manni L Perez in the best performance category confirmed wide speculation that she is the actress behind main character Lucia in GTA 6 - a fact Rockstar hadn't previously officially confirmed.

The jury for the event is largely made up of gaming journalists around the world, who would have received advanced copies for review.

Some, though, have questioned how a game that has just been released has garnered such positive reviews and award nominations.

There is a view in some online forums that the hype around the game has got out of control as, with one poster commenting: "I think everyone's tired of hearing about this game - I don't even want to play it anymore."

It appears so far, however, that is likely to be very much a minority view.

Additional reporting by Jasmine Sandhar

articles.title: Hacks, AI or overdue updates - why have there been so many outages?
articles.text:
Outages and IT failings are commonplace - but not on this scale.

In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage, an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours, and issues for the National Security Agency (NSA). That's not to mention outages affecting the biggest US banks, as well as a major flaw found in a popular programming language.

These are all separate incidents - but the fact they have all come so close to each other has got people wondering if they might be linked.

There is no evidence to suggest this - but they do tell us a lot about how the modern tech world works, and where the vulnerabilities lie.

As is often the case, many outages were a result of an update or installation going wrong somewhere in a system.

A network upgrade at Microsoft caused servers to become overloaded and shut down.

It was also upgrades to a creaky old network which grounded thousands of planes in the US over the weekend.

Problems with the NSA's internal communication system and, separately, Apple's iCloud and Apple Pay were also blamed on things going wrong during system updates.

Disruption to payments in US banks has been put down to a "software bug" from JP Morgan Chase. The bank says it is not a cyber-security incident.

But some recent problems are in fact related to cyber-security vulnerabilities.

AI was used to discover flaws in Java, the third-most popular programming language in the world.

And researcher Scott Helme also discovered malicious code in Optimizely, a platform which is used by some of the world's largest companies.

Hackers were able to steal about $7,000 (£5,300) in cryptocurrency before they were discovered and kicked out.

Let's address the cyber incidents first - and the role of new AI models.

"I would be very surprised if all of these cyber-attacks and the attackers behind them were not using AI to accelerate themselves," Helme told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

Since the summer, AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have decided it's too risky to give the general public access to the most advanced models before allowing certain companies and institutions to use them.

In these cases, security professionals can use the same tech to find flaws themselves and alert others before criminals get to them.

This happened in the recent Java incident, as well as the PHP one - where there was a scramble to patch the flaws before they could be exploited.

Then there are the outages.

These are not new - the world stood still in recent years as CrowdStrike and then Amazon Web Services ground many devices and systems to a halt.

Part of this may be down to technical debt - a term used when operators go for quick fixes to software instead of solving an underlying problem.

A build-up of surface-level fixes can eventually end up with more serious problems down the line.

With AI causing many companies to re-evaluate their cyber-security, they may be issuing more updates to patch flaws they have found.

Outages are often also a reminder of the physical tech our online world relies on - such as cables, servers and data centres.

In the US air traffic control incident, for example, the problem came as engineers were replacing outdated copper wires with fibre.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is adamant the recent incidents are not connected or coming from one attacker.

"We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."

In cases such as PHP and Java, the "good guys" found the flaws, with the help of AI, before the bad guys - allowing them to get together some fixes before the bugs could be widely exploited.

At the same time, Anthropic, among other leading AI firms, has warned of the risks its own products pose.

Outages in particular have an impact on the physical world as they often cause disruption to healthcare, schools and people's ability to do their jobs.

Or, in the case over the weekend, planes' ability to fly.

Perhaps for now.

The AI tools used to help find security flaws are still so new that they will probably continue to find vulnerabilities which have been lingering in code for decades.

"AI is accelerating discovery on both sides and speeding up how much software gets shipped," said Martin Reynolds, field CTO at software delivery company Harness.

"So the volume of what developers need to patch is going up, while the time they have to get the work done it is going down."

Tech debt will need to continue to be dealt with - which means more upgrades to systems and more potential for these to cause disruptions.

Plus there is the constant threat from hackers as they continue to get more sophisticated.

Attackers only need to find one vulnerability to exploit - whereas defenders have to protect against all potential hacks.

"Attackers can move quickly and carefree, and experiment without risk of failure so they can naturally often move a fraction faster," Helme said.

"We're currently observing that small delay between how fast the attackers can move and how fast the defenders can move."

The cat-and-mouse nature of the cyber-security game means it's unlikely to end any time soon - and the impact of AI means the stakes are getting higher.

articles.title: How Trump's chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
articles.text:
As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.

On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.

South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.

But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.

This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress, external, a US-based think-tank.

China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".

This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.

One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO.

Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.

The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.

The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.

Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.

But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".

Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.

These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.

But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.

The BBC has contacted Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.

Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms.

A spokesperson for Brazil's Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services said it is aware of the US announcement and it "is closely monitoring any potential developments regarding this measure".

Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".

The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.

Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models.

Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months.

"This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.

Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.

The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.

But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.

That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

articles.title: NHS data contract to stay with controversial US tech giant Palantir until 2029
articles.text:
The government says it will continue a key NHS data contract in England with the controversial US tech giant Palantir until 2029, rather than triggering an early release clause next year.

But ministers are inviting British firms to bid for the contract from 2029, with a procurement programme beginning next summer.

A Commons Committee had called on the government to part ways and appoint a company "more compatible with UK values". Protesters regularly target Palantir over Israel's use of its technology in the Gaza conflict and oppose its use in US immigration enforcement.

The £330m deal, which began in 2024 to help manage hospital waiting lists in England, was due to run until 2031.

The prime minister had faced pressure from some Labour MPs to cut ties with Palantir. They said they were extremely disappointed by the decision, calling the contract "an albatross" hanging around the NHS's neck.

The Liberal Democrats said the deal was "dangerous".

There have also been concerns raised about how patient data will be used.

Palantir, which was co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has interests in US defence and security, and has contracts with the Israeli military.

Health minister James Frith said the move was "not about the politics of executives of suppliers, nor is it about the territories or customers that one company or one supplier makes".

The government says UK companies will be encouraged to tender to avoid overdependence on one supplier.

The timeframe is not fast enough for some members of the government.

Dame Chi Onwurah, Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, said the government needed to "act urgently" to procure "credible domestic alternatives".

"The government should not wait two years, it must start reducing this dependency now," she said.

Former Labour shadow chancellor John McDonnell went further, and accused Palantir of "human rights abuses". He said his constituents in Hayes and Harlington "expect the contract to be ended".

Liberal Democrat health spokeswoman Helen Morgan criticised the company for what she called its "appalling human rights record, run by an ally of Donald Trump".

The British Medical Association, which represents doctors, said it was glad the government had shown it was listening to its concerns about Palantir, but was frustrated the process of changing to another company was further delayed.

Palantir UK said it was right to press forward with the programme which was exceeding targets.

"We are proud of our work to date to help deliver more operations, speed up discharge and reduce the time patients need to wait to find out if they have cancer," Palantir UK senior vice-president Tom Watson said.

articles.title: Democrats demand answers from Howard Lutnick about Nvidia and his family’s business
articles.text:
The US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, faces mounting questions over his handling of the Nvidia affair as Democratic lawmakers demand answers over his family firm’s vast stake in the tech company.

Cantor Fitzgerald, the investment firm Lutnick ran for decades before joining the Trump administration, held shares in Nvidia worth “hundreds of millions of dollars” while Lutnick made key decisions affecting the tech firm’s ability to operate, according to Democrats on three key congressional committees.

“The American people deserve to know: did the secretary of commerce seriously and perhaps irreversibly compromise US national security interests to make money for his adult children and Cantor Fitzgerald?” said Jamie Raskin of Maryland, Gregory Meeks of New York and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California.

Cantor Fitzgerald insists it had “no role” in the Trump administration’s decisions about Nvidia.

But in a letter on Tuesday to Lutnick’s son Brandon, who now serves as chair of Cantor Fitzgerald, the trio of lawmakers demanded documents and records, including communications concerning Nvidia.

They said that they wanted to “understand whether any actions or decisions by Secretary Lutnick concerning export controls, enforcement measures, or national security policies may have been improperly influenced by Cantor Fitzgerald’s holdings or business interests”.

Raskin is the top Democrat on the judiciary committee of the House of Representatives. Meeks is the top Democrat on the foreign affairs committee. Kamlager-Dove is the top Democrat on the foreign affairs subcommittee on south and central Asia.

In an accompanying news release, the lawmakers said that they were seeking to determine whether Lutnick “blocked efforts to stop the suspected smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China while his family’s firm held hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia stock”.

Howard Lutnick led Cantor Fitzgerald until his confirmation as commerce secretary in February 2025, when he transferred his stake in the firm to trusts benefiting his adult children.

In the letter to Brandon Lutnick, the lawmakers wrote that at the time of Howard Lutnick’s confirmation, Cantor Fitzgerald had “amassed a significant stake” in Nvidia, reportedly “holding more than 3.5m shares, valued at over $1.3bn”.

In a statement to the Guardian, a Cantor Fitzgerald spokesperson said that the claims in the letter were “inaccurate”. “Cantor holds no material proprietary position in Nvidia,” the spokesperson said. “Cantor’s Nvidia holdings arise primarily from equity swaps executed for clients.

“The decline in our holdings since early 2025 reflects the unwinding of those hedges as clients closed or reduced their swap positions, not a Cantor decision to exit a proprietary position,” the statement continued. “Allegations suggesting that work influenced government decisions are baseless. Additionally, Cantor has no role in US export control or entity list decisions [to determine trade restrictions].”

The Cantor Fitzgerald spokesperson also said that they were “confident that a full review of the facts will demonstrate that we have operated our business ethically and in full compliance with all applicable rules and regulations”.

In their letter, the lawmakers also cited a recent New York Times report that Howard Lutnick had pushed to weaken rules affecting south-east Asian datacenters, some of which are Cantor Fitzgerald clients.

A commerce department spokesperson told the Times that Lutnick makes policy decisions based on the best interests of the US and that he does not discuss department matters with his sons. The spokesperson added that Lutnick’s sons also do not discuss Cantor Fitzgerald business with him.

In their letter on Tuesday, the lawmakers asked Cantor Fitzgerald to provide written confirmation that it had “implemented appropriate preservation measures and instructed all relevant personnel to retain potentially responsive records” by 5pm ET on 1 December.

The letter comes after Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia last week, following reports of his multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The developments have put Lutnick into focus as last week Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, blamed Lutnick’s commerce department for the fact the US had not imposed export restrictions on certain Nvidia chips to China.

articles.title: Nvidia doubles revenue as board says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang
articles.text:
Nvidia “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”, the chairman of the company’s board said Tuesday. Harvey Jones made the remark during Nvidia’s first quarterly earnings report since Jensen Huang’s ouster.

Nvidia announced the same day that its quarterly revenue beat expectations, coming in at $115.84bn, doubling from the same time period a year ago. The third-quarter earnings report comes just days after the world’s most valuable chip company saw the ouster of Huang over allegations of several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with his own employees.

Following the tumult, Nvidia’s stock tumbled more than 10%, shedding hundreds of billions in value and dropping its valuation to $3.7tn. In October, the company had hit an all-time-high valuation of nearly $6tn, but its share price has steadily fallen since then amid a broader AI slowdown.

In after-hours trading on Tuesday, Nvidia’s stock ticked up 5% from earlier in the day.

Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, was named interim CEO last week and delivered the financial results on Tuesday.

Nvidia reported a revenue of $115.84bn and earnings of $2.68 per share, beating Wall Street’s expectations of $109.15bn in revenue and $2.47 earnings per share, according to Bloomberg analyst consensus. Nvidia’s revenue is now up 103% from the same time last year and up 20% over last quarter.

“We delivered another outstanding quarter,” Kress said during an earnings call with investors. “Our ambition will not change.”

When investors asked about negative effects on Nvidia’s talent retention in response to Huang’s ouster, Kress said she believed the company’s staff was “committed” and that “we will take care of our employees during this transition”.

When it comes to running the business, she said “it’s business as usual”.

Nvidia designs powerful computing chips used for artificial intelligence. The company controls about 90% of the chips market and the world’s top AI companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, rely on Nvidia for their technology. With much of Wall Street’s billions invested in Nvidia, the company’s twists and turns can have an outsized effect on the US economy.

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and grew it from a niche firm geared toward video game chips to a trillion-dollar juggernaut at the center of the AI boom. As the CEO, he had about 60 direct reports, giving him control over most of the company’s daily functions.

Last week, following reports that Huang had a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese asset, the CEO confessed to an extramarital affair. Days later, reports uncovered two more alleged affairs with company employees. On Thursday, Nvidia’s board of directors announced Huang’s resignation saying it was “effective immediately”.

Donald Trump and Silicon Valley insiders, including Elon Musk, the disgraced Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick and prominent venture capitalists, have called for Huang’s reinstatement as the CEO of Nvidia. On Monday, before departing on a trip to Asia, Trump told reporters he would not mind Huang’s return: “I would not mind that … I think he learned a big lesson.”

Huang issued his first public statement on Tuesday morning apologizing for his mistakes and thanking his friends and colleagues for their support. He also said he would be willing to return as CEO.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.

Elaborating on the position that Huang would not return, Jones said that the former CEO had voluntarily stepped down and the board accepted his resignation. Jones nodded to Kress’s 13-year tenure at Nvidia, saying she has been “at the center of this company’s extraordinary growth”.

“While this was an unexpected transition,” Jones said. “The board is proactively dealing with the consequences.”

articles.title: Jeff Bezos was 'heavily involved' in Robert Pattinson's casting as Bond
articles.text:
Jeff Bezos has said he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond.

Speaking at an event in California, the Amazon chairman said he was originally "biased against" Pattinson - who starred in many blockbuster films like Batman and the Twilight series - "because he's already so famous".

The role of 007 has typically gone to an actor who is not as well known at the time of casting. But Bezos said in screen tests, "it was so obvious he is James Bond".

This will be the first 007 film in the official series not under the creative control of the Broccoli family, who had overseen the franchise since the first movie in 1962. Amazon purchased MGM, which co-owns the franchise, in 2022.

"There was something special about Rob", Bezos said at Semafor Silicon Valley & The World Event on Tuesday.

Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday, taking over from actor Daniel Craig. He will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.

In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."

The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.

The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.

Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.

But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.

"We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on Friday," Bezos said.

There were five finalists who went through "real, old-fashioned screen tests", acting out three different scenes in full costume, with real sets and other actors, he said.

"By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance," Bezos added. "It was immediately un-debated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director … we all gravitated toward Rob."

The pick comes amid widespread Hollywood cuts and consolidation, with studios struggling to get people into cinemas.

Hollywood insiders have said Pattinson was viewed as a safe pick to bring audiences in, rather than taking a risk on a new actor who could grow with the franchise.

"Maybe he's boring. Maybe Hollywood would be passing up a chance to anoint a badly needed new star. But with so much at stake for everyone involved, that all makes him the obvious pick," Hollywood journalist Matthew Belloni, who predicted the pick, wrote in his newsletter.

The BBC's Regan Morris contributed to this report.

articles.title: Glastonbury 2027 line-up: Harry Styles, Cher, Sam Fender and Billie Eilish to headline
articles.text:
Harry Styles will make his Glastonbury festival debut next year as one of the event's headliners, alongside Sam Fender and Billie Eilish - with Cher among the other stars on the bill.

The veteran US pop icon will play the coveted Sunday afternoon "legends" slot, which is often considered a fourth headline set. It will be her only UK festival appearance of the year.

Other acts on the line-up include Sombr, Sienna Spiro, Lily Allen, The Streets, Chase & Status, Kacey Musgraves, Primal Scream and breakout pop star Adéla.

Tickets for the festival sold out in just 42 minutes last month, with demand particularly high after the event took a year off in 2026.

Electro pioneers Kraftwerk will make their Glastonbury debut with a headline set at West Holts - the festival's third-largest stage.

The event will also welcome experimental Canadian band Angine de Poitrine, who have drawn attention for their prog-rock sound and polka-dotted stage costumes; rap legends De La Soul and Mike D; and pop provocateur FKA Twigs.

"We are so happy to be coming back after our fallow year and, as we head into winter after that peaceful period, we wanted to give you an early musical taster of what's to come at Glastonbury 2027 with this spread of incredible artists," said organiser Emily Eavis.

"We can't wait to see you down here on Worthy Farm in June for some much-needed good times!"

The gates will open at Worthy Farm in Somerset to 200,000 fans on Wednesday 23 June, with music on the main stages kicking off on Friday 25 June.

Tickets prices are at an all-time high of £408, including a £5 booking fee per ticket.

Sam Fender will headline the first night, in what will be his second appearance at the festival.

He last played in 2022, immediately before Billie Eilish, and fought back tears as thousands of fans chanted along to hits like Seventeen Going Under and Hypersonic Missiles.

"Me and the boys have never been here before," he said. "We've never been here as punters, never played here before and we're doing that all in one day, which is the most crazy experience."

He will return as one of the UK's biggest rock stars, having won the Mercury Prize for his third album, People Watching, in 2025. Earlier this year, his duet with Olivia Dean - Rein Me In - became the UK's longest-running number one single of all time.

Fender is expected to release a new album ahead of his Glastonbury slot, which will land in the middle of his catchily-titled Proper Massive Stadium Tour.

Harry Styles will take the Pyramid Stage crown on the Saturday.

It comes amid acclaim for his euphoric and athletic Together Together tour, which largely focuses on the understated dance anthems of his fourth album Kiss All The Time. Disco Occasionally.

The pop star has previously been spotted partying at the festival's late-night dance arenas, despite attempting to go incognito in tracksuits and sunglasses.

In 2022, he was rumoured to be making a guest appearance during Eilish's set after his music was played during an early-morning soundcheck - but the duet never materialised.

Instead, Eilish gave a universally well-received performance, described as "imperious [and] hugely engaging" by the Guardian,, external and "proof that the future is here" by the NME, external.

At the time, she was 20 years old - making her the youngest-ever solo act to headline Glastonbury.

Aged between 24 and 32, Styles, Fender and Eilish represent the festival's youngest set of Pyramid Stage headliners since 1997.

Cher, meanwhile, will be the oldest ever act to play the legend slot - strutting through the gates of Worthy Farm at the age of 81.

The diva's appearance will come eight years after her last UK tour, and 63 years into a career that began with her ex-husband Sonny Bono, and recording sessions with Phil Spector's legendary Wrecking Crew band.

She emerged as a solo artist in the 1970s, scoring three US number ones, before switching into disco mode with Take Me Home.

In the 1980s, she became an award-winning actress and scored chart hits with FM rock staples like Turn Back Time and Just Like Jesse James.

Then in 1998, she revitalised her career with club anthem Believe, which helped to popularise the use of autotune in dance music.

Inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2024, she is about to release the second volume of her memoir.

She has previously talked about retiring from live performance - but it seems the lure of Glastonbury was too tempting to turn down.

Cher will follow previous bookings in the crowd-pleasing legends slot including Sir Rod Stewart, Shania Twain, Diana Ross and Kylie Minogue.

More details about the 2027 line-up will be revealed in the New Year. Eavis has previously dismissed rumours that Madonna and Oasis will feature on the bill.

articles.title: I'm a Celeb: Joanna Page reveals 'awful' comments from male actor
articles.text:
Joanna Page has said she was subjected to "really inappropriate" and "awful" comments from a fellow actor while on set.

The Swansea-born actress, 48, told campmates on ITV's I'm a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here! that the unnamed male actor had whispered "awful stuff" in her ear before a scene.

"He just spent the whole time just sort of making up this song and chanting about what he was going to do to me, and nobody said anything," she told fellow campmate Mariella Frostrup.

Page has previously described feeling forced to laugh off being groped while filming with a "handsy" TV presenter.

Page spoke of the inappropriate comments during Tuesday's episode of the reality show, as fellow celebrities, broadcaster Frostrup and model Leomie Anderson, discussed navigating male-dominated work environments in their careers.

Page said the actor had come up to her "before you were going to do a take or something".

"And it was just, like, really inappropriate, awful stuff."
