articles.title: Julio Iglesias faces court investigation over alleged sexual offences
articles.text:
Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff members

Two women, who worked for the 83-year-old in the Caribbean, have accused him of abuse which they say took place in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic in 2021.

The announcement comes after Spanish prosecutors dropped an inquiry into the claims earlier this year after concluding that they lacked jurisdiction because the alleged crimes took place abroad.

Iglesias, who has been a household name in Spain since the 1960s and has sold millions of records worldwide, has previously denied the allegations.

But in a statement published on Wednesday, external (in Spanish), national court Judge Antonio Piña said the account given in the complaint, alongside preliminary evidence provided, justified opening criminal proceedings.

He added that the investigation would cover parts of the complaint relating to potential crimes against sexual freedom, as well as assault and degrading treatment.

But the court will not investigate claims made in the lawsuit of human trafficking or crimes against workers' rights. Piña said these allegations were dismissed after he looked into the hiring of the women and found there was "no deception or artifice involved".

Piña said the former employees had been summoned to testify in person on 3 February.

The announcement comes after Spain's public prosecutor's office shifted its position last month, saying it now believed the court had jurisdiction to investigate the allegations.

In its statement, the national court said Spanish law sets out that courts can hear cases of crimes committed abroad by Spanish citizens provided certain conditions are met.

The allegations against Iglesias first emerged in a joint three-year investigation between Spanish newspaper El Diario, external and television network Univision news, published in January.

In that investigation, the two women were identified as a domestic worker and a physical therapist, who described alleged sexual abuse and degrading working conditions.

The domestic worker, whose name was changed to Rebeca in the reports, said Iglesias would regularly call her to his room at the end of the day and would touch her inappropriately without consent.

Rebeca, a Dominican who was 22 when the alleged events took place, also alleged that Iglesias had forced her to take part in threesomes with another female member of staff. She also described the singer slapping her in the face and grabbing her genitals.

The other woman, a Venezuelan physical therapist named as Laura in the article, said Iglesias had touched her breasts and kissed her on the mouth against her will. She added that he constantly threatened to fire her, controlled how much food she ate and asked her about when her period was due.

Rebeca and Laura filed an initial legal complaint in January against Iglesias for sexual assault and human trafficking.

In a response to the allegations in January, Iglesias said, external: "I deny having abused, coerced, or disrespected any woman. These accusations are absolutely false and deeply sadden me."

On Wednesday, the court said the lawsuit had been accepted based on evidence provided in the complaint. This included a photograph of one of the complainants, showing a bruise on her arm that was "consistent with the possibility of her being grabbed forcefully".

It added that the same photo showed "two marks on one of her thighs that could correspond to a human bite", which the complainant said were "a consequence of her forced participation in acts of a sexual nature".

WhatsApp message exchanges, including New Year's greetings, which suggest an "affectionate" relationship between the women and Iglesias, will also be considered, the court said.

But it added that the seemingly cordial tone, which presents "an apparent discrepancy with certain aspects of the narrative", would be clarified through a "complete and contextualised examination of the communications".

The claim over violations of workers' rights could not be investigated because there is no comparable criminal offence in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic, where the alleged crimes took place, it said.

Iglesias is one of the most successful Latin artists of all time, having sold more than 300 million records in a career spanning decades.

He is also the father of fellow music superstar Enrique Iglesias.

articles.title: Hunger Games prequel Sunrise on the Reaping splits opinion: 'Surreally awful' or 'surprisingly strong'
articles.text:
Reviews of the latest Hunger Games film have seen it dismissed as a "surreally awful prequel" and "a tortuous, costly mess" by some critics - but called "surprisingly strong" and "one of the best films in the series" by others.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth movie in the franchise, and tells the origin story of a teenage Haymitch Abernathy - who was played as an adult by Woody Harrelson.

In a one-star review, the Guardian called the film, external "overwrought and boring", and said it "has no actual interest and no authentic reason to exist, other than to gouge an income stream out of its fanbase".

But the Wrap praised its, external "memorable performances, intoxicating style and horrifying commentary", adding: "When the dust settles it may even be the Hunger Games that holds up best."

Sunrise on the Reaping is set 24 years before the first Hunger Games film, and 40 years after the previous prequel, 2023's The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.

"This prequel lands at some mid-point between Ballad and Hunger Games, which puts it on an immediately odd footing," Empire said in a three-star review, external.

"It can't escape the sense of feeling supplementary. It's an enjoyable-enough diversion, but essentially a footnote with aspirations."

Screen Daily called it, external an "underwhelming prequel", which "suffers from a lack of compelling characters" and "feels oddly incidental - a drab afterthought rather than a crucial new chapter".

articles.title: Ex-rugby player Danika Priim says sex assault 'never happened'
articles.text:
A former England rugby league player and TV pundit accused of putting her hand up a woman's skirt in a cricket club toilet has told a jury it "categorically did not happen".

Danika Priim, 42, has been charged with carrying out the alleged sexual assault in the toilets at Horsforth Cricket Club in Leeds on 22 July 2022.

Her accuser, who cannot be named for legal reasons, previously told a trial at Leeds Crown Court how Priim twice reached up her dress and grabbed her underwear.

Keighley-based Priim, who previously represented Bradford Bulls, Leeds Rhinos and England, including at the 2017 World Cup, denies one count of sexual assault. The trial continues.

Two of the complainant's friends told the court they also witnessed what happened in the toilet but, on Wednesday, Priim told the jury she was never in the toilets with the three women.

Prosecutor Chloe Hudson put it to Priim that there were only two alternatives – either she was lying or the complainant and her two friends were lying.

Priim told the jury: "It categorically did not happen."

The defendant agreed she was not suggesting that it was an accident, or the woman had invited her to touch her, or it was a joke.

Priim told the jury she was never in the toilets with the complainant, adding: "I did not touch (her) in the toilets at all."

Hudson said to her: "What you must be saying is that these three got together to make completely false allegations about you."

Priim responded: "It's the biggest question I have – it's the why."

The prosecutor asked the defendant about how the complainant demonstrated to the jury how she was grabbed.

Priim said: "She was lying. I did not do that."

She added: "I'm also a very happy heterosexual woman. I'm with a man. I live with a man."

The prosecutor said: "The truth is that you sexually assaulted (the woman), didn't you?"

Priim said: "The truth is that it never happened."

articles.title: Channel 4 admits it doesn't know number of Married At First Sight UK sex abuse complaints
articles.text:
Channel 4's chief executive has admitted she doesn't know how many complaints of sexual misconduct were received about Married at First Sight UK, despite a six-month external review into the hit TV show.

When asked by MPs, Priya Dogra said: "I'm not sure I have the details," adding that the review looked specifically at the claims of three women featured in a BBC Panorama.

Married at First Sight UK was cancelled after Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members, while a third woman alleged a non-consensual sex act. The men involved have denied all the allegations.

Separately, Dogra said the broadcaster "cannot apologise enough" to a former employee who twice made complaints about Russell Brand and felt they weren't properly handled.

Dogra said it was "almost unforgivable" that the woman said she complained to Channel 4 in 2009 and again in 2023.

Brand is serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after recently being found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Married at First Sight UK, known as MAFS UK, had been running for 10 seasons and was one of Channel 4's biggest shows, with audience figures often topping three million.

The Panorama investigation in May heard from three women who made allegations about the men they were partnered with - claims the men deny:

One woman said her on-screen husband raped her and threatened her with an acid attack.

A second woman told both Channel 4 and production company CPL, before broadcast, about being allegedly raped by her on-screen husband. Her episodes were still aired.

A third woman accused her on-screen husband of sexual misconduct.

All three women accused the show of not doing enough to protect them.

A review was commissioned into MAFS UK by Channel 4 shortly after the BBC first contacted the broadcaster with details of the allegations.

Earlier this month, the completed review recommended extra safeguards on the show. But Channel 4 said the programme had "run its course" and apologised to the women involved in the investigation.

Speaking to MPs on the House of Commons culture and media committee on Tuesday, Dogra was repeatedly asked if she knew how many allegations Channel 4 and CPL had received over the years that MAFS UK was on air.

"I looked specifically into those instances [the three women], I did not do a broad sweep of every episode or every season of the show. That is not what the terms of reference for the show were," she responded.

"If there are others, we would take them seriously and look into them on the same basis."

Channel 4's bosses were also questioned at length about Brand by MPs in the hearing.

Brand's work on Channel 4 included hosting Big Brother sister show Big Brother's Big Mouth and its celebrity equivalent from 2004 to 2007, a chat show in 2006, and appearing on Big Fat Quiz of the Year.

Addressing Dogra and Channel 4's chairman Geoff Cooper, MPs said the member of staff who made two complaints about Brand "fell through the cracks".

In response, Dogra said: "I'm not sure we can apologise enough as an organisation for putting her through that twice. We have apologised in public in the past and in private."

She accepted that the woman's complaints were "not handled properly" and added that "it's almost unforgivable that happened twice".

When asked by the committee if junior members of staff could raise complaints against a star without fear of losing their job, Dogra replied she "can't say 100%" that that would be the case.

"What I can do is set the standard, set the tone, make sure that the facilities are available, make sure that my staff and the production companies understand the repercussions of not complying, and understand the kind of culture that I'm trying to set, and we're trying to set as an industry."

She also said she found the "cultural personality" around Brand "horrendous".

"I find it distasteful, and I look at the jokes... that is the lowest form of humour, because these are jokes that are made at the expense of someone else's physical safety.

"I don't believe it should have been acceptable then, and I certainly don't think it's acceptable now."

During the session, Dame Caroline also put to Channel 4 bosses that in both the MAFS UK and Brand cases, the broadcaster appeared like "a child with their hand in the cookie jar".

The committee chairwoman asked: "To what extent can you reassure us that Channel 4's priority is genuinely the welfare of the staff who work there, the staff who have worked there, and the people who take part in your shows - rather than purely when the world is looking at you and you suddenly feel that you've got a reputational reason to take a look at these shows?"

Dogra responded by saying that when Channel 4 commissioned the review, "we didn't even know whether the Panorama programme would be made".

She added: "We had received a right-to-reply letter and the programme came out six weeks later, but it equally it could not have been made. We always intended to do the review."

In the instance of the woman who tried to complain about Brand, she added: "I'm not sure there are more apologies we can give. Because none of those things should've happened."

articles.title: Birmingham university pauses Shakespeare Institute move after backlash
articles.text:
The University of Birmingham has paused plans to move the Shakespeare Institute from Stratford-upon-Avon to Birmingham amid growing opposition to the proposal.

The university said it would spend the next six months working with partners including the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) and the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust to explore the institute's future in Stratford.

The decision comes after criticism from Stratford-upon-Avon MP Manuela Perteghella and a petition that attracted more than 12,000 signatures.

The move from its home at Mason Croft had been due to take place in September.

The postgraduate research institute announced on Friday that it had been told it would leave Stratford and relocate to the University of Birmingham's Edgbaston campus, with future plans unclear for its Mason Croft base, historic gardens and playing fields.

Announcing the pause on Tuesday evening, University of Birmingham vice-chancellor and principal Prof Adam Tickell said he had heard "very clearly" how much the institute mattered to Stratford-upon-Avon and the wider Shakespeare community.

"I have therefore decided to pause the planned move as we explore how and whether the Institute can have a vibrant and viable future in Stratford-upon-Avon," he said.

articles.title: 'Human' is the Cambridge Dictionary's Word of the Year
articles.text:
"Human" is the Cambridge Dictionary's Word of the Year — defined as "having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines".

"The growth of AI means it is now necessary to explicitly say 'human' for things that once could only be done by humans," said chief editor Colin McIntosh.

Examples of current usage included actors Scarlett Johansson challenging "an assault on human creativity" and Matthew McConaughey protecting himself against unauthorised digital reproduction of his voice or image.

"The measure of AI's success should be how much it improves human lives," said Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates on learning about the dictionary's choice.

McIntosh said dictionary editors had to be on top of how words could change over time "to reflect what people say and what they write".

His research revealed a four-fold use of the word human since 1900.

"'Man' used to be used in this sense a lot more, but now it is not acceptable to use 'man' to mean men and women," he added.

"Human didn't come into use in Middle English until the 14th Century, from a French word. Shakespeare used it, but after that it was very restricted in use."

There had also been an increased use of compound words such as human-made and human-driven, to distinguish the works, qualities and skills of people from AI.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
articles.text:
In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it.

For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building.

For a long time you really are two-bit criminals on the run, getting in with every dirtbag petty thief and drug-runner you come across in order to scrape some cash together and stay under the radar. You meet hillbilly pill-heads and biker gangs, friendly conspiracy theorists, a shady doctor, Lucia’s former prison friends and their lowlife boyfriends. By the time I actually got to Vice City – a glitzy den of sin, the centre of all Leonida’s pleasures and all its most extravagant criminality, where the gangbangers hustle on social media and even the narcos are obsessed with their Instagram clout – I had been playing for 30 hours. It took me 70 hours to finish the game and I could have taken longer.

Leonida is so lifelike that at times it beggars belief, so vast that it feels overwhelming, and outside the story missions you can do whatever you please. There are nightclubs, gyms, flea markets, malls, restaurants, clothes shops, basketball courts, shooting ranges, aircraft hangars, projects and mansions, places to hunt and fish or go kayaking, gas stations and thousands of individuals engaged in conversation as you pass by. Interesting things are always happening in your peripheral vision. You might witness the cops chasing someone down to plant drugs on them, or overhear an interesting confrontation, or see a car speeding away and wonder where it’s going – though interesting things always seemed to happen when I was driving a stolen car at high speed towards a discerning buyer, or otherwise unable to stop and follow my nose. Thankfully, another opportunity would always present itself.

I often felt that the only thing messing up Rockstar’s perfect simulation was me. All this detail and realism comes with some disadvantages, namely complex controls and a tendency for the game’s systems to collide with my intentions in unexpected and sometimes annoying ways. Here I am, driving at high speed through the city before clipping the kerb and flipping my car, causing a massive pile-up. Here I am pressing the wrong button and accidentally punching a random passerby rather than greeting them as intended, kicking off a ridiculous skirmish in which I have to knock out half the customers at a restaurant before running from the cops. Here I am again pressing the wrong button at a bike rack and ending up pinned beneath a tumbling row of bicycles. Missions can go south very quickly and for reasons that aren’t always obvious. In every street race I wiped out spectacularly by crashing into something I couldn’t properly see, while my opponents magically recovered from every collision and sped ahead. This can be a frustrating game at times: unpredictable, laborious, unwieldy and, occasionally, unfair. That is because you are not the master of the game world. You simply exist within it.

Like most compelling crime fiction, Jason and Lucia’s story involves an escalating series of messy events that pull them further and further from where they started, and have you constantly wondering how on earth they’re going to get out of the newest trouble they’re in. To avoid spoilers, substantive discussion of this story can only happen in the coming weeks. But I will say that I was rooting so hard for Jason and Lucia by the end that I felt quite sick with worry about what was going to happen to them, pacing back and forth in front of my TV throughout the final missions. Among all the expectations I had for GTA VI, I did not expect it to make me so emotional.

The key to this is the bond you form with Jason and Lucia. After tens of hours in their company, watching them together – how she smiles fondly at him when they dance together, their playful banter, the stick-ups they pull off as a duo, their resilience and faith in themselves and each other in the face of escalating disaster – I found it impossible not to care for them. They are our avatars in GTA VI’s world but they are not blank stand-ins for the player: you decide their actions but not their personalities. They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim. It made me care about them much more. When the story gave me opportunities to decide what would happen next, what came to mind for me was what they would do, not what I would do.

This is indicative of a tonal shift for Grand Theft Auto that became more obvious the more I played. This series is famous for its violence, misanthropy and pitch-black humour. I have been invested in its characters before, have even rooted for some of them, but I have rarely liked them or related to them. This is the first GTA that wants to encourage some measure of empathy alongside its trademark violent chaos. I was astonished to discover that the game offers you small incentives for acts of kindness, such as texting your partner a selfie, doing your neighbour a favour or throwing your rubbish in the bin rather than dropping it on the ground. Jason and Lucia are not extravagant caricatures, but two people trying to make it in a world totally stacked against them. Pretty much everyone in this Floridian fever-dream is a total crook, on the take or mixed up in some bullshit scheme. It’s so easy to get away with crime in this city, and so difficult to do things the right way. The events of this game might be totally outlandish but these characters and their motivations keep things at least somewhat grounded.

If you thought this newfound heart might tone down GTA’s 18-rated provocativeness, however, you would be very wrong. The protagonists may be surprisingly relatable but they exist in a world that is absurdly foul-mouthed, filthy and over-the-top offensive in every imaginable way. I have never played a game that has more thoroughly earned its 18 rating. Barely a half-hour ever goes by without someone snorting coke off a knife blade, or some full-frontal nudity. There are missions set inside a pornographer’s mansion and a small-town strip club; you can visit those clubs and get a private dance (as either Jason or Lucia, for what it’s worth, or together). At one point Lucia opens the wrong hotel room door to see a woman in a corset wielding a golf club, thwacking balls at a guy’s testicles. On the in-game TV there is a reality show about horny geriatrics. It does not so much push the boundaries of taste as ignore the existence of taste. It contains every perverted scenario you could imagine and several more that would never occur to you.

Sometimes it is a little jarring to emerge from a really pivotal and moving scene between Jason and Lucia into a virtual city where the billboards read things like “WANTED for shitting everywhere: THE SHIT BEAST.” But I found these two sides of GTA’s personality surprisingly easy to accommodate. It’s not as though the story is without its many moments of absurd levity and humour, too: at one point I was taking a bunch of terrifying gang leaders with face tattoos on a real-estate tour, where they sincerely admired the outdoor space with brick pizza oven, and another time I was chasing a man wearing nothing but an alligator thong through a well-to-do suburban neighbourhood. A game this huge can accommodate both pathos and lewdness, and much more.

I did find, however, that Lucia – Grand Theft Auto’s first female protagonist – changed how a lot of this landed for me. GTA has never been particularly kind to women (or men, for that fact, but in past games it has exclusively been the women who were sexualised). There is still a lot of sexism in GTA VI’s world, but now we have Lucia to react to it. This is the first GTA in which I have felt the women are treated as people, not only Lucia but also the many other female characters in the story, from up-and-coming rappers to Lucia’s mother, from a jaded strip-club worker to a badass middle-aged drug-runner whose custom purple carbine rifle is her prized possession. This is a game in which women can be as violent, visibly tough and deeply messed-up as the men. And without wanting to give too much away: there are male strippers in Leonida, too.

I am not about to make a case for GTA VI as a feminist game – there is much to be offended by here, if you are so inclined – but I will say that as a woman who has played and enjoyed every GTA game while also often rolling my eyes at their casual sniggering misogyny, GTA VI hits different for me. I liked it more because the women aren’t always the butt of a joke. Also for the first time, I did not find the violence gratuitous or overblown, despite the fact that this is a story about crime and criminals. There is nothing here like GTA V’s infamous torture mission, which made me feel sick. It says a lot that of all the immoral opportunities afforded to me in Vice City, the only thing I straight-up said “no” to was getting involved in a metaverse scam. THAT would be going too far.

I keep reaching for something that sums up GTA VI, as much as it’s possible to sum up a game as vast as this, and the closest I come is the nightclubs. These show GTA VI at its most extravagant: hundreds of virtual people under the pulsing lights, all dressed up to go out, dancing to a fastidiously curated soundtrack featuring some of the real world’s most famous artists as the controller pulses to the bassline in your hands. These big nights out are an opportunity for both Vice City’s sleaziest denizens and Rockstar’s developers to flash their cash: they are the game’s most ostentatiously expensive and showy scenarios. But at the centre of it all, there are Jason and Lucia, dancing together, focused on each other in the midst of all this chaos and excess.

articles.title: ‘I hope paramedics are on standby for the sex scenes!’ The wet and wild TV experience leaving fans dizzy
articles.text:
I’m in the cinema foyer when I first spot them: hockey jerseys. Lots of them. “I’ve no idea what to expect!” giggles Chloe, who is wearing a black and yellow “Rozanov” jersey. Like me, she has never been to a 4DX screening before – but when Cineworld announced it would be showing episodes five and six of queer hockey drama Heated Rivalry in the novel format, she booked tickets immediately. “I actually had tickets for the 2D screening, but cancelled them for this,” she says.

Over the last two weeks, Heated Rivalry fans have been treated to big screen marathons of Jacob Tierney’s hit TV show, based on Rachel Reid’s bestselling book series, Game Changers. But 4DX is next level. The “extreme sensory” cinema technology is usually deployed for high-octane action flicks – films with epic battles or chase sequences. Still, with Cineworld offering the opportunity to “immerse yourself in the motion, wind, water [and] scent” of major league hockey’s raunchiest fictional romance, who could resist?

“I’m a big fan of Heated Rivalry; last weekend, I watched all the episodes at the cinema in one day – then they advertised the 4DX screenings,” says Ross. “I’ve never been to a 4DX screening before, so I thought this was the perfect opportunity.”

Will it be hot – literally? And steamy? Will it … vibrate? “The mind boggles!” says my seat neighbour, Ann – also wearing a jersey, this time in the red, white and blue of Shane Hollander’s Montreal Metros. She’s here with a group of Heated Rivalry megafans she met on the social media platform Threads, nine of them in total. They’ve been to a few fan events together, but 4DX is a first for her, too. “I hope they have paramedics on standby for the sex scenes!” she laughs. “I know there’s a bit in a swimming pool, so maybe we’ll get wet – whoah! We’re moving!”

The adverts come to a close and suddenly we’re off – thrown up and down in our seats, spritzed with water and blasted with cool air. I clutch my armrests and look for a seatbelt; there isn’t one. The screening is only half full – some men, mostly women – but soon everyone is hysterical with laughter. This, we realise, is going to be silly … and it’s going to be fun.

If you thought Heated Rivalry was all erotic tension and clandestine rendezvous, think again: 4DX soon makes it clear it’s actually all about texting. Every message – and there are a lot of them – sends a vibration through the seat. It’s like being sat on the sofa with someone in a particularly incessant group chat. Doors, too, now appear to be opened and closed more regularly, and with vibrational intent. When Hollander suffers a fractured collarbone and concussion on the ice, 4DX does its best to replicate the experience – and it is not exactly pleasant.

Plus, ice hockey is cold. Russia, where Ilya Rozanov’s family live, is really cold. And yes, when Shane and Ilya flirt by splashing each other with water in a lake, you end up damp.

Some of it makes more sense. As New York Admirals captain Scott Hunter beckons Kip Grady down from the stands in the penultimate episode’s heart-thumping climax, gentle seat movements make the moment feel genuinely dizzying. Someone behind me likens it to seasickness, but each to their own. Whether or not the inevitable bed-bouncing and, er, thrusting were in any way enhanced is also debatable.

“In reality, it was probably the thing that was least necessary to watch in 4DX – but that actually made it better because it was so daft,” says Alice, who I meet on the way out. She has come with her friend Hayley – both genuine hockey fans and season ticket holders who decided to book the screening while watching a game last week. “You can see the people who made it must have been thinking: well, what have we got? We’ve got doors, we’ve got cars, he’s in the snow for like 0.5 seconds, so let’s do something with that! We were crying with laughter.”

“Every time there was water on screen, you were just bracing yourself,” adds Hayley.

Indeed, when I ask cinemagoers about their favourite bits, most collapse into sheepish laughter. There is a particular scene that clearly springs to most minds – although, personally, it was one squirt of water I could have lived without. “That bit was quite the experience – I was absolutely mortified!” says Lindsey, one of the Threads group. She had a great time, though she concedes that “the effects maybe took away from the emotional aspect a little”.

As for Chloe, who swapped 2D for 4DX – did it live up to expectations? “It was brilliant!” she says, beaming. “I hope they do more. I’d definitely come again.”

articles.title: Kelly Gough is simply astounding as Desire Under the Elms reaches the heights of Greek tragedy
articles.text:
You would not know that Eugene O’Neill’s play was originally set on a mid 19th-century farm. This version by director Ebenezer Bamgboye brings modernity with its sleek storytelling, but also nods to the ancient Greek drama O’Neill was emulating in his 1924 play about illicit desire and the father-son fight for land.

It makes for a strange mix at first, beguiling and bewildering in equal measure. Bamgboye employs some of the striking theatricality that he brought to his magnetic adaptation of The Lonely Londoners two years ago. It is an original refashioning, the script sharper with less of the exposition that might date it, but the directorial flourishes come so thick and fast that it is stylised to the bone. Bamgboye has previously worked with Rebecca Frecknall (who staged the leaden O’Neill drama A Moon for the Misbegotten last year) and the first half seems to pay too big a debt to her style of work.

Ephraim (Antony Byrne) is an irredeemably tyrannical father and Eben (Zackary Momoh) his calculating son. Eben sees off his two half-brothers in hope to claim this farm, passed down from his late mother, as his own, when Ephraim brings home a young new bride, Abbie (Kelly Gough). “I can’t believe all this is mine,” she says, crowingly, when she sees the farm. So begins the fractious relationship between Abbie and Eben.

There is an attempt to tell O’Neill’s story on another level, with a racial element added. Set in the deep south rather than its original north-east, the dynamic is that of a white father and Black son through its casting. Eben speaks of his father’s slave-driving and his wrongful ownership of stolen land; Ephraim’s iron-rod rule begins to look like that of a plantation owner.

As in Frecknall’s production of A Streetcar Named Desire, music interprets emotion, from screams to sexual overtures and angry clashes. A live, roving trumpet and guitar interject in these moments, the musicians stalking the auditorium like musical ghosts, along with the spectre of Eben’s dead mother, singing languorously.

Movement is key, with sex or violence also transposed to dance, or jagged, jittery twitches. The effect is sometimes arresting but also overwrought. The sexual chemistry between Eben and Abbie is so choreographed that it does not give off enough heat. The ghostliness and gothicism seems over-egged with smoke rising from the blank canvas of darkness on Basia Bińkowska’s non-realist stage design.

But it rights itself and the overload of manufactured expressiveness gives way to something far more elemental in the second half when this production allows its actors simply to act. Momoh is good but Gough (whose sister Denise played the same role in a production 14 years ago) is off the scale. Part-Phaedra, part-Medea, she is a woman who has a purity of desire alongside her steeling ambitions and strength: she is the one to activate the attraction she feels towards Eben. Her unravelling is painful to watch, and her performance really does rise to the heights of Greek drama, intense and unstoppably tragic.

The tension takes on a vice-like grip as the music, movement and gothicism come together. This is artistic director Rupert Goold’s final production before his departure and is not perfect yet it rises to become incredibly powerful.
